Teaching model, not a diagnosis. Real systems involve hundreds of genes, many cell types and feedback loops. Solid = established mechanism · dashed = association in groups · dotted = hypothesis.

: Twin studies estimate heritability around 74%. Genome-wide studies find many common variants, each with a very small effect; 27 loci reached significance in the largest study, with 76 candidate genes enriched for expression in early brain development.
: Rare protein-truncating variants and copy-number changes add risk in some people. The 2023 study implicated SORCS3 through both common and rare variants.
: An estimated 84–98% of ADHD-influencing variants are shared with other psychiatric conditions — one reason ADHD so often co-occurs with others, and why genes cannot diagnose an individual.
: The enzyme that makes L-DOPA from tyrosine — the usual rate-limiting step in making dopamine and noradrenaline.
: Pumps dopamine from the cell fluid into storage vesicles, ready for release. Amphetamines disturb this storage and redistribute dopamine into the cell fluid.
: Recaptures released dopamine, ending its signal. Methylphenidate blocks it; amphetamines can reverse it so it pushes dopamine out.
: Recaptures noradrenaline — and in the prefrontal cortex, where DAT is sparse, much of the dopamine too. Atomoxetine blocks it.
: Enzymes that break dopamine and noradrenaline down inside and outside cells.
: Receive the dopamine signal. D2 receptors on the releasing cell also act as a brake (autoreceptors), feeding back to reduce release.
: Noradrenaline receptors in prefrontal cortex that strengthen task-relevant network signals. Guanfacine stimulates them.
: Tyrosine → L-DOPA → dopamine (→ noradrenaline in noradrenergic cells).
: Dopamine is packed into vesicles; unpacked dopamine is vulnerable to breakdown.
: Vesicles release their contents when the cell fires. Amphetamines add a second, firing-independent release route.
: Transporters pull the signal back in; enzymes break it down. Most medicines act by slowing clearance or forcing release.
: Autoreceptors and adaptation adjust the system over time. Transporter levels appear to shift after stimulant exposure — which complicates brain-scan comparisons.

: Prefrontal cortex regulates attention, behaviour and emotion; imaging shows these regions less active, with weaker connections, in ADHD on average. Its function depends on finely tuned dopamine and noradrenaline levels.
: In 223 children with ADHD versus 223 controls, half of cortical points reached peak thickness by about 10.5 years versus 7.5 years — a delay most marked in prefrontal regions.

: Across 23 sites, accumbens, amygdala, caudate, hippocampus and putamen were slightly smaller on average (effect sizes d −0.11 to −0.19), mainly in children; differences in adults were not significant. Medication did not explain them.

: In 53 unmedicated adults, PET showed lower dopamine transporter and D2/D3 receptor binding in reward regions, correlating with inattention. But a meta-analysis found transporter levels lower in drug-naive and higher in previously medicated people — so findings depend on history.
: Holding a goal, inhibiting distractions, switching and planning. Common-variant ADHD risk is associated with weaker performance on several executive measures.
: How strongly future or delayed outcomes drive effort now.
: Matching alertness to the task — too little or too much both degrade control.
: Knowing what to do and not being able to begin — one of the most commonly described ADHD difficulties.
: Losing track of a plan between deciding and doing; forgetting why you entered a room.
: Under-estimating elapsed time and time needed; 'now' and 'not now' as the only two clocks.
: Speech or action running ahead of evaluation.
Many common variants → Cortical maturation timing:
— Risk genes are enriched for early brain development expression; the route to cortical timing is not demonstrated.
Many common variants → Reward pathway markers:
— Common-variant risk is associated with midbrain dopaminergic neuron expression (Demontis 2023).
— Individual rare-variant routes are mostly untested.
— Whether transporter differences are a cause or an adaptation to past medication is unresolved (Fusar-Poli 2012).
Reward pathway markers → Reward and motivation:
— Individual differences in vesicle storage capacity shaping stimulant response is a research question, not an established ADHD mechanism.
: Blocks dopamine and noradrenaline transporters, so released transmitter stays active longer. First-line in children and one of two first-line options in adults (NICE).

: Enter the terminal, disturb vesicle storage and run transporters in reverse, releasing dopamine and noradrenaline independent of firing; they also block reuptake. In adults' clinician-rated trials, amphetamines had the largest average symptom effect, with lower tolerability than placebo.

: An inactive prodrug absorbed intact and converted to d-amphetamine, mainly by red blood cells. Same active drug as dexamfetamine, delivered more gradually — a different exposure profile, not an identical one.
: Non-stimulant that blocks the noradrenaline transporter, raising noradrenaline and prefrontal dopamine.
: Non-stimulant that stimulates alpha-2A receptors in prefrontal cortex, strengthening network signalling.
The useful way to think about it:
the parts are few, the regulation is complex.
Most people with ADHD do not have a broken part; they have many small differences in how parts are built and tuned, adding up across development.

articles.description: On average, the brain in ADHD matures on a later timetable, especially in prefrontal regions, with small differences in some deeper structures — largest in childhood.
articles.statusNote: Body, figures and links extracted from the pinned file. Wording was not rewritten.
articles.text: MJB ADHD home · Guidebook MJB ADHD · Static reading view · Interactive version Brain development and structure Status: sourced · Content checked 2026-10-06 On average, the brain in ADHD matures on a later timetable, especially in prefrontal regions, with small differences in some deeper structures — largest in childhood. Quick understanding Brain-imaging studies do not show an "ADHD brain" you could spot on a scan. They show average differences between large groups: the cortex reaches its peak thickness later, and some deeper structures are slightly smaller in childhood. Research finding strong Across 824 scans of 223 children with ADHD and 223 controls, half of the cortex reached peak thickness by about 10.5 years in ADHD versus 7.5 years in controls; the delay was greatest in prefrontal regions that control attention and motor planning. R4 Research finding strong Pooling 23 sites (1, 713 people with ADHD, 529 controls), the accumbens, amygdala, caudate, hippocampus and putamen were slightly smaller on average (d −0.11 to −0.19); differences were largest in children, not significant in adults, and not explained by stimulant medication. R3 Possible explanations The pattern fits a developmental timing account: the same sequence of maturation, running later. Smaller differences in adults suggest partial catch-up for many people — while symptoms can persist, consistent with function depending on more than size. Deeper explanation Effect sizes of around 0.1–0.2 mean the two groups overlap almost completely. These are clues about mechanism, not tools for diagnosis. Uncertainty Most large studies are cross-sectional; true lifespan trajectories need longitudinal data. Sources cited R4 Shaw P, et al. ADHD is characterized by a delay in cortical maturation. articles.title: The dopamine and noradrenaline supply chain
articles.description: Six steps — make, store, release, clear, break down, self-tune. Simple parts; the complexity is in regulation, timing and how the steps interact.

articles.text: MJB ADHD home · Guidebook MJB ADHD · Static reading view · Interactive version The dopamine and noradrenaline supply chain Status: sourced · Content checked 2026-10-06 Six steps — make, store, release, clear, break down, self-tune. Simple parts; the complexity is in regulation, timing and how the steps interact. Quick understanding Think of a supply chain. A factory makes the product (synthesis), a warehouse stores it (vesicles), a shipping dock releases it (firing), a recycling crew collects what is left (transporters), a disposal service breaks down the excess (enzymes), and a manager watches demand and adjusts output (autoreceptors). Step Main part What can vary Make Tyrosine hydroxylase Rate, regulation by demand Store VMAT2 Capacity and leakage Release Vesicle fusion; amphetamine reverse transport Amount per signal Clear DAT, NET Speed of recapture Break down MAO, COMT Speed of disposal Self-tune D2 autoreceptors; adaptation Feedback strength over time Research finding strong Amphetamines release catecholamines by redistributing them from vesicles to the cell fluid and reversing plasma-membrane transporters, alongside effects on uptake, exocytosis, synthesis and metabolism. R8 Possible explanations Why "bottleneck" is a useful word — and where it misleads. In any chain, output is limited by the slowest step. That makes it tempting to look for one broken step in ADHD. The evidence points instead to many small differences spread across steps and across brain regions, adding up. Hypothesis A "component bottleneck" framing — ADHD as instability arising from several mildly under-performing components rather than one failure — is a useful way to think about individual differences in treatment response. It is a framework for generating testable questions, not an established model. Research finding strong In prefrontal cortex, where dopamine transporters are sparse, noradrenaline transporters clear much of the dopamine, and alpha-2A receptors strengthen task-relevant signals — so attention depends on balance, not simply on "more". R9 Treatment logic Each medicine targets a different step: methylphenidate slows clearing ; amphetamines force release and slow clearing; atomoxetine slows noradrenaline clearing; guanfacine strengthens prefrontal reading of the signal. Different steps, different timing, different side-effects — see How ADHD medicines act . Deeper explanation Too little and too much both impair prefrontal function — an inverted-U relationship. That is one reason doses are titrated, why the same dose can feel too strong one day and too weak another, and why "more" is not reliably "better". Research finding moderate Transporter levels appear to adapt to stimulant exposure, being higher in previously medicated people — the system re-tunes itself to treatment. R6 Existing site library Continue in the existing MJB library . Uncertainty Most mechanism detail comes from cells, animals and small imaging studies. Which step matters most for any one person cannot currently be measured. Sources cited R8 Sulzer D, et al. Mechanisms of neurotransmitter release by amphetamines: a review. articles.title: Genetics — many small influences
articles.description: ADHD is highly heritable, but through thousands of common variants of tiny effect plus rarer variants in some families. Genes describe risk in populations, not a diagnosis in a person.

articles.text: MJB ADHD home · Guidebook MJB ADHD · Static reading view · Interactive version Genetics — many small influences Status: sourced · Content checked 2026-10-06 ADHD is highly heritable, but through thousands of common variants of tiny effect plus rarer variants in some families. Genes describe risk in populations, not a diagnosis in a person. Quick understanding ADHD runs in families. Most of that is genetic, but not in the "one faulty gene" sense. It is closer to height: many variants, each nudging the odds slightly. Research finding strong Family, twin and adoption studies show ADHD runs in families, with twin heritability around 74%; about a third of heritability is attributed to many common variants of small effect, and rare copy-number variants account for part of the rest. R7 A variant or medication response alone does not establish a neurological diagnosis. Read diagram text A genetic result is a laboratory finding (orientation N6, N7). A clinical pattern comes from history and examination. A medication response is a clue, not proof. Specialist interpretation reads them together. A variant or a medication response alone does not establish a neurological diagnosis. The album gene-to-symptom fault tree is held. Possible explanations Research finding strong The 2023 genome-wide meta-analysis identified 27 loci, implicated 76 genes enriched in early brain development, found a higher burden of rare protein-truncating variants in a set of risk genes (implicating SORCS3), and linked common-variant risk to weaker complex cognition and executive function. W5 What this means: genetic risk shapes how the brain develops and runs , mostly through many small effects. What it does not mean: that a genetic test can confirm ADHD, or that any one gene explains a person's symptoms. Deeper explanation The overlap with other conditions is large. That supports the idea that some of the same developmental machinery underlies several conditions, with different combinations producing different presentations — consistent with frequent co-occurrence. Existing site library Continue in the existing MJB library . Uncertainty Individual genetic findings in single people (for example, a variant found on a panel test) need specialist interpretation; most variants are of uncertain significance. articles.title: No single dopamine story
articles.description: Different studies point to different parts of the system, and some findings depend on medication history. ADHD is better described as several routes to a similar set of difficulties.
articles.statusNote: Body, figures and links extracted from the pinned file. Wording was not rewritten.
articles.text: MJB ADHD home · Guidebook MJB ADHD · Static reading view · Interactive version No single dopamine story Status: sourced · Content checked 2026-10-06 Different studies point to different parts of the system, and some findings depend on medication history. ADHD is better described as several routes to a similar set of difficulties. Quick understanding The simple version — "ADHD is low dopamine" — is too simple. Some studies find lower dopamine markers, some find higher, and some differences appear to be adaptations to treatment rather than causes. Research finding moderate In 53 unmedicated adults, dopamine transporter and D2/D3 receptor binding were lower in reward-pathway regions than in controls, and lower binding correlated with inattention. R5 Contested account Across nine imaging studies, transporter density was on average 14% higher in ADHD, but strongly dependent on prior stimulant exposure: lower in drug-naive people and higher in previously medicated people. R6 Possible explanations Several routes : different combinations of genetic and developmental differences can produce similar day-to-day difficulties. Adaptation : the system re-tunes after long-term treatment, changing what a scan shows. Region matters : prefrontal cortex and striatum regulate dopamine differently. Co-occurring conditions add their own signals. Deeper explanation Heterogeneity is not a weakness of the ADHD concept. It is what you expect from a polygenic, developmental condition — and it predicts that people will differ in which medicine, dose and formulation suits them, which is what clinical experience shows. Research finding strong Most ADHD-influencing genetic variants are shared with other psychiatric conditions, supporting overlapping mechanisms rather than a single dedicated pathway. W5 Uncertainty There are no validated subtypes that predict which medicine an individual will respond to. Sources cited R5 Volkow ND, et al. articles.text: MJB ADHD home · Guidebook MJB ADHD · Static reading view · Interactive version Explore evidence Status: drafted · Content checked 2026-10-06 Genes, brain development, the dopamine and noradrenaline machinery, treatment trials — and the open questions still being argued. Start here The evidence pages are ordered as a ladder: start with the overview, then climb down a level at a time — genes, development, the synapse, treatment trials — until you reach the questions nobody has answered yet. Each level states what is established, what is an association in groups, and what is still a hypothesis. ADHD and biology — the overview — ADHD is supported by converging genetic, developmental, brain and treatment evidence. There is no single cause and no diagnostic brain or gene test — but the core machinery is well understood. Genetics — many small influences — ADHD is highly heritable, but through thousands of common variants of tiny effect plus rarer variants in some families. Genes describe risk in populations, not a diagnosis in a person. Brain development and structure — On average, the brain in ADHD matures on a later timetable, especially in prefrontal regions, with small differences in some deeper structures — largest in childhood. The dopamine and noradrenaline supply chain — Six steps — make, store, release, clear, break down, self-tune. Simple parts; the complexity is in regulation, timing and how the steps interact. No single dopamine story — Different studies point to different parts of the system, and some findings depend on medication history. ADHD is better described as several routes to a similar set of difficulties. What treatment trials show — Randomised trials show the medicines reduce core symptoms in adults; a withdrawal trial shows frequent symptom relapse in previously stable adult lisdexamfetamine responders after switching to placebo. Registries suggest wider outcomes may improve, with important caveats. Open research questions — Five live questions arising from one person's observations — each with competing explanations and the observations that would tell them apart. Questions, not conclusions, and never a reason to self-experiment. Dystonia: patterned twisting and spasms — Dystonia is a movement disorder involving involuntary muscle contractions. This page helps you describe a pattern for assessment; a twisting sensation alone does not establish the diagnosis. Coordination and balance: understanding ataxia — Ataxia describes impaired coordination. A description of imbalance is a starting point for assessment, not proof of one inherited or degenerative condition. Hereditary spastic paraplegia: what assessment looks for — HSP is a group of genetic conditions. This page explains why clinicians consider it and why a symptom resemblance or isolated genetic result is insufficient. Dopamine-responsive dystonia: a distinct clinical question — Dopa-responsive dystonia is a specific group of movement disorders. Improvement with an ADHD medicine is not equivalent to the clinical levodopa response used in its assessment. A field guide to the nervous system — Start with the affected function, the clinical pattern and the decision you need. Follow the evidence beyond slogans about a single chemical. Parkinson’s: symptoms, treatment, genetics and care — A practical guide to recognition, motor and non-motor symptoms, treatment choices, medication continuity, genetics and research, with sources and questions to take to a specialist. FND: diagnosis, active treatment and accountable care — Real symptoms deserve a positive diagnosis, symptom-specific rehabilitation, accessible support and a reviewed plan. Understand the options and what the treatment trials actually show. Further routes Start the A field guide to the nervous system for condition patterns and an audit of familiar explanations. c: Genes, brain development, the dopamine and noradrenaline machinery, treatment trials — and the open questions still being argued.

The evidence pages are ordered as a ladder: start with the overview, then climb down a level at a time — genes, development, the synapse, treatment trials — until you reach the questions nobody has answered yet. Each level states what is established, what is an association in groups, and what is still a hypothesis.
— ADHD is supported by converging genetic, developmental, brain and treatment evidence. There is no single cause and no diagnostic brain or gene test — but the core machinery is well understood.
— ADHD is highly heritable, but through thousands of common variants of tiny effect plus rarer variants in some families. Genes describe risk in populations, not a diagnosis in a person.
— On average, the brain in ADHD matures on a later timetable, especially in prefrontal regions, with small differences in some deeper structures — largest in childhood.
The dopamine and noradrenaline supply chain
— Six steps — make, store, release, clear, break down, self-tune. Simple parts; the complexity is in regulation, timing and how the steps interact.
— Different studies point to different parts of the system, and some findings depend on medication history. ADHD is better described as several routes to a similar set of difficulties.

— Randomised trials show the medicines reduce core symptoms in adults; a withdrawal trial shows frequent symptom relapse in previously stable adult lisdexamfetamine responders after switching to placebo. Registries suggest wider outcomes may improve, with important caveats.

— Five live questions arising from one person's observations — each with competing explanations and the observations that would tell them apart. Questions, not conclusions, and never a reason to self-experiment.
— Dystonia is a movement disorder involving involuntary muscle contractions. This page helps you describe a pattern for assessment; a twisting sensation alone does not establish the diagnosis.
— Ataxia describes impaired coordination. A description of imbalance is a starting point for assessment, not proof of one inherited or degenerative condition.

— HSP is a group of genetic conditions. This page explains why clinicians consider it and why a symptom resemblance or isolated genetic result is insufficient.

— Dopa-responsive dystonia is a specific group of movement disorders. Improvement with an ADHD medicine is not equivalent to the clinical levodopa response used in its assessment.

articles.text: MJB ADHD home · Guidebook MJB ADHD · Static reading view · Interactive version Open research questions Status: drafted · Content checked 2026-10-06 Five live questions arising from one person's observations — each with competing explanations and the observations that would tell them apart. Questions, not conclusions, and never a reason to self-experiment. Quick understanding Good questions are the end point of an evidence trail. Each one below starts from an observation, lists several explanations, and names what would distinguish them. None is established; none should change anyone's treatment on its own. Not a protocol Nothing here suggests altering medicines, combining products, or testing ideas on yourself. The tests named are ones a clinician or researcher would design and supervise. The questions Q1 · Could a hereditary movement disorder explain dopamine-responsive movement symptoms? Patient observation Matthew reports that walking, posture and spasm were markedly better on dexamfetamine and worsened when it stopped; genetic testing for a hereditary spastic paraplegia has been discussed. AUTHOR-ACCOUNT Research finding limited Reviews describe juvenile or early-onset parkinsonism with variable levodopa response mainly in SPG7 and SPG11, alongside dystonia and ataxia in several types. R13 Research finding limited Single case reports describe SPG7 with levodopa-responsive parkinsonism and with loss of dopamine-transporter signal on imaging. R12 R14 Competing explanation What would point towards it A genetic movement disorder with a dopamine component A pathogenic variant confirmed by a specialist; dopamine-transporter imaging findings Two unrelated conditions Movement findings independent of medication timing Indirect benefit (energy, effort, organisation) Improvement in effort-dependent tasks but not in tone or reflexes Musculoskeletal or functional contributors Specific examination findings Observable test: structured, clinician-observed movement measures at matched times, with a specialist interpreting any genetic result. Q2 · Do differences in vesicle storage shape stimulant response? Hypothesis Individual differences in VMAT2 storage capacity or leakage might change how much an amphetamine can release, and so how strongly someone responds. This is not an established ADHD mechanism. Research finding Amphetamines act partly by disturbing vesicle storage, so storage is mechanistically relevant to their effect. R8 Competing explanations: absorption and conversion differences; dose; adaptation after long treatment. Observable test: research imaging of vesicle transporters exists but is not a clinical tool; in practice, carefully recorded dose–response at a stable time of day is the usable proxy. Q3 · Can a tablet's ingredients change response to the same drug? Patient observation Matthew reports a consistent difference between generic dexamfetamine 5 mg and Amfexa 10/20 mg. AUTHOR-ACCOUNT Clinical guidance Amfexa 10 and 20 mg tablets contain no povidone or crospovidone; Amfexa 5 mg contains crospovidone. W4 Competing explanations: different total dose; different timing; expectation; manufacturer differences other than excipients. The Amfexa 5 mg tablet is a natural test case for the povidone idea, because it is the same brand with a crospovidone ingredient. Observable test: pharmacist-confirmed products, same strength and timing, consistent records over repeated normal use. Q4 · Does pain or physical strain draw on the same control capacity as attention? Hypothesis Physical strain may compete for the same limited regulatory capacity, so cognitive symptoms worsen on high-pain days. Competing explanations: poor sleep from pain; low mood; sedating pain medicines. Observable test: daily ratings of pain, sleep and specific cognitive slips over several weeks, analysed together. Q5 · Is there an energy threshold below which the supply chain falters? Hypothesis Vesicle loading depends on an ATP-driven proton gradient; if cellular energy supply were limited, storage might falter under sustained demand, producing worse function late in the day or after exertion. Competing explanations: ordinary fatigue, deconditioning, sleep debt, medicine wearing off. Observable test: whether worsening tracks exertion and time-since-dose separately, recorded consistently. Evidence and sources Every research claim here comes from case reports, reviews or mechanism studies. Case reports show something can happen; they cannot show how often, or whether it explains one person. Uncertainty All five are open. Some may be wrong. They are included because a well-framed question is more useful to a clinician than a confident guess. Unresolved sources Genetic test results, specialist neurology assessment and dispensing history are needed before Q1 and Q3 can be advanced in this case. articles.text: MJB ADHD home · Guidebook MJB ADHD · Static reading view · Interactive version What treatment trials show Status: sourced · Content checked 2026-10-06 Randomised trials show the medicines reduce core symptoms in adults; a withdrawal trial shows frequent symptom relapse in previously stable adult lisdexamfetamine responders after switching to placebo. Registries suggest wider outcomes may improve, with important caveats. Quick understanding Three kinds of study answer three different questions: Question Study type Answer so far Do the medicines reduce symptoms? Randomised controlled trials Yes, in children and adults R2 Does benefit last only while taking them? Randomised withdrawal trials Relapse was frequent after switching stable adult lisdexamfetamine responders to placebo; this does not mean every patient relapses R1 Do they change real-world outcomes? Registry studies emulating trials Starting is associated with fewer serious outcomes W2 W3 Possible explanations Research finding strong In adults, amphetamines (SMD −0.79), methylphenidate (−0.49), bupropion and atomoxetine beat placebo on clinician-rated symptoms at about 12 weeks; head-to-head, amphetamines were more efficacious than methylphenidate and atomoxetine; tolerability was lower than placebo for amphetamines and methylphenidate. R2 Research finding strong Adults stable on lisdexamfetamine for at least six months, randomised to continue or switch to placebo, relapsed at 8.9% versus 75.0% over six weeks, mostly within two weeks. R1 Research finding strong Starting medication was associated with lower two-year all-cause mortality (HR 0.79) and unnatural-cause mortality (HR 0.75), but not natural-cause mortality. W2 Deeper explanation Registry studies cannot fully rule out that people who start treatment differ in ways that also lower risk. Target-trial emulation reduces this, but does not remove it. Short trials measure symptoms; registries measure events. Neither measures the long-term effect of withdrawing an established treatment in adults — that gap is real. Uncertainty Long-term randomised evidence in adults is limited; the strongest long-term outcome data are observational. Sources cited R2 Cortese S, et al. Each route ends in something usable. The idea behind this guide Simple parts, complicated control The machinery that ADHD medicines act on is made of a small number of parts: an enzyme that makes dopamine, a pump that stores it, a release step, transporters that clear it, enzymes that break it down, and receptors that read it. That short list is the same in every textbook. What varies between people — and what makes ADHD hard to pin down — is how those parts are built, tuned and coordinated across development and across a day. This guide is organised the same way: a few clear entrances at the top, then progressively finer detail, until each route ends at a decision, a question or a piece of evidence you can check. Start with how ADHD works , or with what to do when treatment stops . What this guide will not do It will not diagnose anyone, tell anyone to change a dose, or present a hypothesis as a finding. Where the evidence runs out, the page says so and turns the gap into a question. Uncertainty The guide combines sourced explanations, documented accounts and open research questions. It is not an exhaustive assessment of every cause or treatment. Sources cited

This page helps you describe a pattern for assessment; a twisting sensation alone does not establish the diagnosis. Quick understanding Clinical guidance Dystonia can produce spasms, twisting movements and unusual postures. It may affect one region or more of the body. Choice depends on the dystonia type and assessment. N1 Deeper explanation A useful treatment question is what function should improve: comfort, head position, walking or an everyday task. articles.text: MJB ADHD home · Guidebook MJB ADHD · Static reading view · Interactive version FND: diagnosis, active treatment and accountable care Status: sourced-draft · Content checked 2026-10-07 Real symptoms deserve a positive diagnosis, symptom-specific rehabilitation, accessible support and a reviewed plan. Understand the options and what the treatment trials actually show. A diagnosis should open a care pathway Our recommendation is direct: FND should lead to an active, individual care plan. “Nothing more to do” is not a rehabilitation plan. Ask for an explanation of the diagnosis, appropriate treatment options, someone responsible for coordination, and a review date. This is the site's advocacy position; it does not promise that a particular intervention will work for everyone. Clinical guidance Functional neurological disorder describes problems with nervous-system functioning that can produce disabling neurological symptoms. Diagnosis should be supported by positive clinical features, rather than inferred solely from normal investigations. FND-NHS Institutional position King's College Hospital describes assessment, explanation and individually selected treatment, including specialist physiotherapy, psychological therapy and multidisciplinary rehabilitation. Its service also explicitly recognises that FND can coexist with other neurological illness and should not prevent treatment of that illness. FND-KINGS Start with the symptom and the activity it prevents. A useful next request is: “What can we start now, who will arrange it, and when will we review whether it is helping?” Use the depth controls to read only the section you need today. Understanding and checking the diagnosis Real symptoms, explained properly FND symptoms are experienced as involuntary. A functional explanation is not permission to accuse someone of pretending, dismiss their disability or stop listening. Patients should be able to ask how the diagnosis was reached without being treated as obstructive. Clinical guidance FND can include movement, sensory and seizure-like symptoms. It can occur alongside another neurological condition. The clinical pattern and examination matter; a normal scan alone does not establish the diagnosis. FND-NHS Clinical guidance The speech and language therapy consensus also recommends diagnosis using positive clinical features. Its approach treats functional communication and related symptoms as problems requiring assessment and intervention. FND-SLT Ask the diagnosing clinician to document: Which positive findings support FND in my case? Which symptoms does that explanation cover, and which remain unexplained? What other diagnoses or coexisting conditions were considered? What change would trigger reassessment or a different investigation? Can I have the explanation and next steps in writing? A positive diagnosis does not require every person to have the same history or presumed cause. Do not force an account of trauma onto someone as the price of being believed. Discuss relevant physical, psychological and social factors respectfully, with the person's consent and individual history in view. A useful explanation includes a route forward An explanation should connect the examination findings with the proposed treatment. A metaphor about signals can help, but it should not replace that reasoning. Ask the team to explain what the therapy aims to change and what improvement would look like in everyday life. Where uncertainty remains, record it accurately. “FND is supported by these signs, but this new problem still needs assessment” is more useful than treating one label as a permanent answer to every future symptom. See My case: who owned the next decision? and Prepare for an appointment . Match treatment to the problem Rehabilitation is more than generic exercise advice Clinical guidance The physiotherapy consensus recommends education, movement retraining and self-management in a supportive, non-judgemental setting. It addresses attention and movement patterns as part of treatment, and includes referral and discharge within a coordinated package. FND-PHYSIO For movement symptoms, ask whether the therapist understands functional motor problems and can explain the approach. A specific movement or activity goal is more useful than an unexplained instruction to exercise harder. Agree manageable practice, adjustments and what to do when symptoms worsen. Clinical guidance The occupational therapy consensus centres education, rehabilitation through everyday activities and taught self-management. It describes occupational therapy as part of multidisciplinary care, rather than an optional afterthought once other referrals have failed. FND-OT For daily function, bring one or two activities that matter: washing, preparing food, leaving home, returning to study or managing work. Ask for help with the barriers and practical adaptations. Support and rehabilitation can be planned together; a person should not have to wait for complete recovery before basic access needs are recognised. Clinical guidance Speech and language therapy consensus recommendations cover functional voice, speech, swallowing, cough and related symptoms. Education and symptom-specific treatment are delivered within a supportive therapeutic relationship; the recommendations are expert consensus, not proof that one technique reliably works for everyone. FND-SLT Main difficulty Route to discuss A practical question Weakness, tremor or disrupted walking Physiotherapy with FND knowledge What movement will we retrain, and how will progress be measured? Daily tasks, participation and routines Occupational therapy Which activity can we make safer or more manageable first? Voice, speech or swallowing Speech and language therapy What assessment and symptom-specific intervention are appropriate? Functional seizures A coordinated neurology and relevant therapy plan What is the diagnosis, episode plan and treatment goal? Several interacting problems Multidisciplinary rehabilitation Who coordinates the plan and reviews competing needs? The table summarises routes discussed in the clinical service and consensus sources FND-KINGS FND-PHYSIO FND-OT FND-SLT . It is a conversation guide, not an individual referral decision. Psychological treatment should have an explained purpose Psychological care can be an active part of treatment. Ask what it targets: seizure-related difficulties, symptom management, distress, mood, a relevant trauma history or another agreed problem. Being offered it should not mean physical symptoms are imaginary, and it should not automatically close access to appropriate rehabilitation. Institutional position The King's service includes both physiotherapy and psychological approaches, and considers coexisting mood conditions and alternative diagnoses. It describes the choice of treatment as individual. FND-KINGS Do not turn uncertainty into unsupervised drug trials. Ask for a medication review with a clear target, expected benefit, possible harms and follow-up. Medicines prescribed for a coexisting illness require their own clinical decisions; this guide does not supply a medicine or dose to treat FND itself. What the treatment evidence actually says Physiotherapy: compare the real alternatives Research finding moderate Physio4FMD compared a specialist intervention with community neurological physiotherapy. At 12 months, the primary physical-function outcome did not show a significant between-group advantage. Some secondary outcomes favoured specialist treatment, including perceived improvement and confidence in the diagnosis. FND-TRIAL The comparison was rehabilitation versus rehabilitation. It was not a trial showing that neglect is equivalent to active care. Equally, the secondary findings do not overturn the primary result or establish that specialist physiotherapy guarantees recovery. Ask how the proposed programme fits your symptoms, access needs and goals. Research finding moderate The report notes disruption from COVID-19, different treatment waiting times and reliance on participant-reported outcomes. These limitations matter when interpreting the results and deciding what further research is needed. FND-TRIAL Functional seizures: separate symptom counts from other benefits Research finding moderate CODES compared seizure-specific CBT plus standardised medical care with standardised medical care alone. It did not find a significant advantage on the primary monthly seizure-frequency outcome at 12 months. Several secondary outcomes improved, including functioning, perceived improvement and aspects of quality of life. FND-CODES Research finding moderate Secondary comparisons were not adjusted for multiple testing. Those results support a more qualified discussion of potential benefit, rather than a blanket claim that CBT stops functional seizures. FND-CODES The trial concerned a particular adult seizure population. It does not establish the answer for every FND symptom, child or person with coexisting epilepsy. Treatment goals should name the outcome being sought, not simply say “better.” Consensus and trials answer different questions The physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech and language documents provide expert recommendations for what care can involve. They are not interchangeable with randomised evidence of effectiveness. The two trials above add important comparisons but leave unanswered questions about matching treatment to individuals, access, long-term outcomes and alternatives when an approach is unsuccessful. Our recommendation is to offer a reasoned, monitored care pathway while being honest about those limits. An unsuccessful intervention should trigger review of the plan, rather than an automatic judgment that the patient did not try hard enough. See How evidence is labelled . Make the plan concrete and reviewable What to ask for before the appointment ends The following is the site's practical advocacy checklist, informed by the care routes above. It is not a statement that every local service provides every intervention or that referral guarantees acceptance. Explanation: the supporting findings, symptoms covered and unresolved questions. Treatment: the appropriate rehabilitation or therapy route and its agreed target. Ownership: the clinician or team responsible for coordination and review. Access: who submits the referral, how acceptance is checked and who handles delays. Interim support: a realistic plan for daily function, safety and access while waiting. Review: a date, meaningful goals and the response if treatment is ineffective or intolerable. Reassessment: which new features require further assessment and whom to contact. For a declined referral, request the reason in writing and the proposed alternative. A waiting list is a service status, not a complete interim care plan. If responsibility is transferred, ask the receiving team to confirm it has accepted the handover. See Transfers, shared care and Right to Choose , When treatment stops and Who is responsible? . Measure something that matters to the person Choose a small number of goals without turning self-monitoring into another exhausting task. Examples include safely managing one household activity, tolerating a shorter journey, communicating a need more reliably or recovering more effectively after an episode. Agree the method with the therapist and adapt it when it becomes unmanageable. A fluctuating condition requires flexible planning. Bring fatigue, pain, sensory needs and other conditions into the discussion. Ask how appointments, practice and communication will be adapted. Support should be judged by what it helps someone do and how tolerable it is, rather than attendance or optimism alone. If symptoms change or an episode occurs Ask for an individual written episode plan that family, carers and relevant services can understand. It should explain the established diagnosis, usual pattern, appropriate response and when urgent assessment is needed. Do not assume a new collapse, injury or altered episode is the same as previous functional symptoms. Seek urgent assessment for a new serious neurological problem or immediate danger. FND should not become a reason to disregard new symptoms or a coexisting illness. Emergency decisions require the current situation and clinical assessment, not a label read from an old letter. Sources, service access and next steps Read for a specific purpose NHS Inform: FND — public explanation and treatment routes; indexed excerpts checked here. King's College Hospital: FND service — an example of active clinical assessment and treatment. Its published referral route is restricted to GPs in South East London, not a nationwide self-referral option. Physiotherapy consensus — principles of movement rehabilitation, education and self-management. Occupational therapy consensus — daily activities and participation. Speech and language therapy consensus — communication and related symptoms. Physio4FMD report — the actual rehabilitation comparison and limitations. CODES trial — functional-seizure treatment outcomes and interpretation. Use Prepare for an appointment to turn one difficulty into a concrete request. Use A field guide to the nervous system for neighbouring conditions and Parkinson’s: symptoms, treatment, genetics and care for the separate Parkinson's pathway. These conditions can require different investigations and treatments; the shared care principle is explanation, appropriate action and continuity. The conclusion is practical: acknowledge the disability, explain the diagnosis, consider appropriate active treatment, adapt access and review the outcome. Leaving a person with a label and no workable next step is a failure of planning, not a satisfactory care recommendation. articles.text: MJB ADHD home · Guidebook MJB ADHD · Static reading view · Interactive version Parkinson’s: symptoms, treatment, genetics and care Status: sourced-draft · Content checked 2026-10-07 A practical guide to recognition, motor and non-motor symptoms, treatment choices, medication continuity, genetics and research, with sources and questions to take to a specialist. Start with the whole picture Parkinson’s is often described as a dopamine problem. That helps explain an important treatment target, but it is too small a description of the person’s experience. This guide connects recognition, daily function, treatment and continuity of care. Use the depth controls to stop at the detail you need. Clinical guidance Parkinson’s involves damage to dopamine-producing nerve cells in the substantia nigra. The cause is usually not known; age, genetic susceptibility and environmental factors are involved. Dopamine loss is part of the explanation, not a test you can perform on yourself. F10 Clinical guidance Movement problems can coexist with pain, fatigue, sleep disturbance, bowel or bladder difficulties, and changes in mood or thinking. Symptoms and their impact vary between people and can fluctuate within a day. PD-SYM If you need one useful next step: describe what has changed, when it began, which everyday activities are affected, and what decision you need from the care team. A clear account of function can be more useful than choosing a mechanism first. Recognition and diagnosis What a specialist is trying to establish Clinical guidance Diagnosis is based on the history and a detailed examination. F11 Clinical guidance Characteristic features include slow movement, rigidity and tremor, often starting on one side. The condition can also affect balance, cognition and mood. PD-GEN A useful appointment record separates what you experience from what was found on examination . “My leg feels stiff” and “the examiner documented rigidity” are different pieces of information. Ask the clinician to explain the examination findings in plain language. Parkinson’s, parkinsonism and other movement problems Clinical guidance Parkinsonism describes a movement pattern rather than one single cause. Some medicines, vascular disease and other neurodegenerative conditions can produce parkinsonian features. Identifying the cause requires clinical assessment. PD-DIFF A label shared between conditions does not make their causes, prognosis or treatments interchangeable. A treatment response is an observation to document, not permission to choose or escalate a drug independently. Not everyone has the same combination. The functional effect may be more important to the person than how conspicuous a symptom appears. PD-SYM For your own notes, choose a few activities you can describe without exhausting yourself: getting out of a chair, turning, dressing, writing, using cutlery or walking through a doorway. Record what is difficult and what helps. If you use video, agree how the clinician can receive it securely. Clinical guidance Sleep difficulties can have several forms, including insomnia, daytime sleepiness and acting out dreams during REM sleep. Parkinson’s symptoms and medicines can contribute. Describe the pattern to the care team so it can be assessed rather than treated as one generic sleep problem. PD-SLEEP Clinical guidance Swallowing problems can affect eating, drinking and saliva management. Difficulty swallowing, repeated coughing with meals or changes in intake should be discussed promptly; a speech and language therapist can assess swallowing and support a safer plan. PD-SWALLOW A sudden new problem needs timely clinical assessment rather than a long reading exercise. Report abrupt deterioration or new confusion to the responsible team; use emergency services for immediate danger. When they do not, choices can include levodopa, a dopamine agonist or an MAO-B inhibitor, discussed with the person. A practical guide to recognition, motor and non-motor symptoms, treatment choices, medication continuity, genetics and research, with sources and questions to take to a specialist.

Parkinson’s is often described as a dopamine problem. That helps explain an important treatment target, but it is too small a description of the person’s experience. This guide connects recognition, daily function, treatment and continuity of care. Use the depth controls to stop at the detail you need.

Parkinson’s involves damage to dopamine-producing nerve cells in the substantia nigra. The cause is usually not known; age, genetic susceptibility and environmental factors are involved. Dopamine loss is part of the explanation, not a test you can perform on yourself.

Movement problems can coexist with pain, fatigue, sleep disturbance, bowel or bladder difficulties, and changes in mood or thinking. Symptoms and their impact vary between people and can fluctuate within a day.

articles.text: MJB ADHD home · Guidebook MJB ADHD · Static reading view · Interactive version When treatment stops Status: sourced · Content checked 2026-10-06 A gap in a treatment that was working can quickly undo its benefit. Here is what the evidence does and does not show, and how to plan for continuity. Quick understanding When an ADHD medicine that was helping stops, symptoms can return quickly. In the selected adult responders studied below, most relapses after switching to placebo occurred within two weeks. A planned break, agreed with a clinician and reviewed, is different from an unplanned gap caused by a broken pathway. The aim of this page is to help you get a timely, reasoned decision either way. Research finding strong In a randomised withdrawal trial of adults stable on lisdexamfetamine for at least six months, 75% of those switched to placebo relapsed within six weeks, compared with 8.9% who continued — most relapses happened in the first two weeks. R1 A request framework, not a guarantee of prescribing or a legal determination. Read diagram text Ask, in writing: named owner; interim plan; reasons and alternatives; review date; escalation route if there is still no owner. Not a guarantee of prescribing. Not a legal determination. Editorial framework for the continuity and no-prescriber routes. W1 is ADHD guidance context only and does not specify this five-box form. Possible explanations Why does benefit fade so fast? Stimulants act within hours and are cleared within hours; they do not "build up" a lasting store of benefit. So stopping removes the effect on the next day's symptoms, not months later. Why might harms follow? Large registry studies show that people with ADHD who start medication have lower rates of several serious outcomes than similar people who do not start. Those studies are about starting, not stopping — but they explain why clinicians and patients take unmet need seriously. Research finding strong Among 148,578 people in Sweden newly diagnosed with ADHD, starting medication within three months was associated with lower two-year all-cause mortality (39.1 vs 48.1 per 10, 000; HR 0.79), driven by unnatural causes such as injuries, poisoning and suicide. W2 Research finding strong In a matching analysis, starting treatment was associated with fewer first episodes of suicidal behaviour (IRR 0.83), substance misuse, transport accidents and criminality — but not accidental injuries — with larger reductions in people who had had previous events. W3 Research finding moderate In UK primary-care records, adults with diagnosed ADHD had an apparent life-expectancy gap of about 6.8 years (men) and 8.6 years (women) compared with matched controls. R11 What these studies do not show They compare people who started treatment with people who did not. They do not measure what happens when an established, working treatment is withdrawn, and their numbers should not be reversed into an estimate of withdrawal harm. They support concern and planning — not a calculated risk for any individual. Useful next action Before or during any gap, get these five answers in writing. The next page has a request you can build and copy. Who will make the next prescribing decision? What records of previous benefit and side effects will they receive? What checks or reassessment are needed, and who arranges them? What is the interim plan and review date, and what happens if function deteriorates? If shared care is not accepted, who supplies the medicine? Clinical guidance NICE asks that medication review include the effects of missed doses, planned dose reductions and periods of no treatment, and that the reasons for continuing are documented. W1 Treatment logic A restart after a gap is a clinical decision, not an administrative one. It should weigh the documented previous benefit, the reasons the gap happened, current physical and mental health, and the safest way to re-establish the dose. See Restarting after a gap . Institutional position In one case, a trust declined a "bridging" prescription on the grounds that restarting at the previous dose after several weeks off, outside an active treatment plan, would not be safe without a new assessment and titration plan. AUTHOR-ACCOUNT That reasoning is common and can be legitimate. The question it leaves is timing : if reassessment is required, who provides it, and how soon? Deeper explanation Interruption has several common causes in the UK, none controlled by the patient: national supply shortages; GP practices declining shared care (which places responsibility back with the specialist); discharge without a receiving prescriber; prescription lengths that do not match re-order rules; and substitution between products. Each produces a gap through a different broken link — and each needs a different fix. Institutional position Ministers have said GP practices may decline shared care, with responsibility then remaining with the specialist service. P5 Institutional position The independent ADHD Taskforce found ADHD under-recognised and under-treated in England. W8 Evidence and sources Study type What it tells you Main limitation Randomised withdrawal trial R1 Symptoms return quickly when an effective treatment is swapped for placebo Short; symptom scores, not injuries or deaths Target trial emulation of starting treatment W2 W3 Starting medication is associated with fewer serious adverse outcomes Observational; about starting, not stopping Life-expectancy cohort R11 The baseline risk in diagnosed UK adults is high Diagnosed adults only; no medication data Guidance W1 What review should include Does not guarantee a particular prescription Continue in the existing MJB library . Useful questions If a gap has happened, what is the earliest date someone will make a prescribing decision? What made the treatment work before, in specific, recordable terms? Uncertainty The sources assembled here do not establish the long-term harm of forced interruption of an established ADHD treatment in adults. The size of any risk for a particular person cannot be calculated from these studies. Unresolved sources Within-individual Swedish analyses of on- and off-treatment periods and UK shortage surveys are cited in earlier drafts but not yet re-checked for this register. gap caused by a broken pathway. The aim of this page is to help you get a timely, reasoned decision either way.

a.aria-label: Research finding, confidence strong: show sources

c: In a randomised withdrawal trial of adults stable on lisdexamfetamine for at least six months, 75% of those switched to placebo relapsed within six weeks, compared with 8.9% who continued — most relapses happened in the first two weeks.

a.alt: Five-step written request: named owner, interim plan, reasons and alternatives, review date, escalation route.

c: A request framework, not a guarantee of prescribing or a legal determination.
Ask, in writing: named owner; interim plan; reasons and alternatives; review date; escalation route if there is still no owner.
Not a guarantee of prescribing. Not a legal determination. Editorial framework for the continuity and no-prescriber routes. W1 is ADHD guidance context only and does not specify this five-box form.

Why does benefit fade so fast? Stimulants act within hours and are cleared within hours; they do not "build up" a lasting store of benefit. So stopping removes the effect on the next day's symptoms, not months later.
Why might harms follow? Large registry studies show that people with ADHD who

medication have lower rates of several serious outcomes than similar people who do not start. Those studies are about starting, not stopping — but they explain why clinicians and patients take unmet need seriously.

a.aria-label: Research finding, confidence strong: show sources

c: Among 148,578 people in Sweden newly diagnosed with ADHD, starting medication within three months was associated with lower two-year all-cause mortality (39.1 vs 48.1 per 10, 000; HR 0.79), driven by unnatural causes such as injuries, poisoning and suicide.

a.aria-label: Research finding, confidence strong: show sources

c: In a matching analysis, starting treatment was associated with fewer first episodes of suicidal behaviour (IRR 0.83), substance misuse, transport accidents and criminality — but not accidental injuries — with larger reductions in people who had had previous events.

a.aria-label: Research finding, confidence moderate: show sources

c: In UK primary-care records, adults with diagnosed ADHD had an apparent life-expectancy gap of about 6.8 years (men) and 8.6 years (women) compared with matched controls.
What these studies do not show

They compare people who started treatment with people who did not. They do not measure what happens when an established, working treatment is withdrawn, and their numbers should not be reversed into an estimate of withdrawal harm. They support concern and planning — not a calculated risk for any individual.
Before or during any gap, get these five answers in writing. The
has a request you can build and copy.
Who will make the next prescribing decision?
What records of previous benefit and side effects will they receive?
What checks or reassessment are needed, and who arranges them?
What is the interim plan and review date, and what happens if function deteriorates?
If shared care is not accepted, who supplies the medicine?
NICE asks that medication review include the effects of missed doses, planned dose reductions and periods of no treatment, and that the reasons for continuing are documented.

A restart after a gap is a clinical decision, not an administrative one. It should weigh the documented previous benefit, the reasons the gap happened, current physical and mental health, and the safest way to re-establish the dose. See

In one case, a trust declined a "bridging" prescription on the grounds that restarting at the previous dose after several weeks off, outside an active treatment plan, would not be safe without a new assessment and titration plan.
That reasoning is common and can be legitimate. The question it leaves is
: if reassessment is required, who provides it, and how soon?

Interruption has several common causes in the UK, none controlled by the patient: national supply shortages; GP practices declining shared care (which places responsibility back with the specialist); discharge without a receiving prescriber; prescription lengths that do not match re-order rules; and substitution between products. Each produces a gap through a different broken link — and each needs a different fix.
Ministers have said GP practices may decline shared care, with responsibility then remaining with the specialist service.
The independent ADHD Taskforce found ADHD under-recognised and under-treated in England.
Symptoms return quickly when an effective treatment is swapped for placebo
Short; symptom scores, not injuries or deaths
Target trial emulation of starting treatment
Starting medication is associated with fewer serious adverse outcomes
The baseline risk in diagnosed UK adults is high
Diagnosed adults only; no medication data
Does not guarantee a particular prescription
Continue in the existing MJB library
If a gap has happened, what is the earliest date someone will make a prescribing decision?
What made the treatment work before, in specific, recordable terms?

The sources assembled here do not establish the long-term harm of forced interruption of an established ADHD treatment in adults. The size of any risk for a particular person cannot be calculated from these studies.

articles.text: MJB ADHD home · Guidebook MJB ADHD · Static reading view · Interactive version When medication feels weak, inconsistent or inert Status: sourced · Content checked 2026-10-14 Check the exact product, delivery, timing and function before drawing a conclusion. A repeated difference deserves review; its cause is a separate question. Start with the product and the benefit If a prescribed medicine feels weak, inconsistent or as though it does nothing, the explanation may be that it does not suit you. But useful questions also concern what was supplied, how it delivers the active drug, when you assessed it, interactions and the function you wanted to improve. A lack of benefit alone does not establish an allergy, poor absorption or a defective tablet. Same active ingredient. Different tablet. Potentially a different experience. Record an apparent difference precisely, then ask a pharmacist and prescriber to review it. Patient observation Looking back at my earlier treatment, I experienced much better everyday function with Amfexa 10 mg and 20 mg tablets than with the generic dexamfetamine 5 mg tablets I had previously been given. I rarely collected the earlier product because I experienced little useful benefit. This is my retrospective account; it is not a controlled comparison or a recommendation for somebody else. AUTHOR-ACCOUNT Hypothesis I wondered whether povidone or a related ingredient contributed to that difference. I have not isolated the ingredient from the other differences between products and treatment periods. This remains a question, not a demonstrated mechanism or an allergy diagnosis — see Open research questions . What else could change the experience? Product differences deserve consideration alongside dose, time course, sleep, pain, other medicines and daily demands. More than one factor may be involved. Question Information that helps a review Was the same active drug, strength and dose supplied? Box, pharmacy label, manufacturer, strength and dispensing record Was the release system different? Immediate or modified release; when benefit began and ended Did timing, food or another medicine change? A simple dated account, rather than guessing from memory Was the desired benefit the same? Initiation, attention, persistence, motor function and unwanted effects recorded separately Did sleep, pain or the task itself change? What else was different on the relevant days An improvement in concentration is not automatically an improvement in every other symptom. Equally, a day with little useful function does not directly measure the drug's blood concentration. Retrospective impressions are valuable starting points; repeated observations and dispensing records can help test alternative explanations. Check the pack and ask a specific question Write down the exact name, manufacturer, strength and dosage form . Include the product licence number (PL) if available. Different strengths of one brand can have different ingredients. Read the product's Patient Information Leaflet. Its contents section lists the other ingredients. In the clinician-facing Summary of Product Characteristics, look at section 6.1: List of excipients . Record what changed and when: product, prescribed dose, time taken, meals, other medicines, expected benefit, observed benefit, duration and adverse effects. Ask your pharmacist to confirm which product was dispensed. Ask your prescriber whether a formulation change, interaction review or another clinical assessment is appropriate. Find UK product information on emc . Bring a photograph of the pack or pharmacy label if remembering its name is difficult. Keep any comparison clinician-led Do not change doses, stop treatment or crush, split or dissolve a medicine to test an explanation unless your pharmacist or prescriber confirms that the specific change is appropriate. Product score lines and release properties differ. What excipients do — and what the lists show An excipient is a medicine ingredient other than the active substance, included for a particular purpose. Fillers, binders, disintegrants, lubricants, coatings and colourants are examples. Some ingredients have recognised effects or tolerability implications; an ingredient's presence does not make the product inferior. EXC-EMA Institutional position European regulatory information recognises that some excipients can have effects in particular circumstances and requires corresponding ingredient and safety information. This supports checking the actual formulation; it does not demonstrate the cause of one person's poor response. EXC-EMA The following comparison uses the named UK manufacturer documents checked on 14 October 2026. It concerns ingredient lists, not comparative efficacy. Named product Listed excipients Product information Amfexa / Dexamfetamine Sulfate Medice 5 mg Isomalt, crospovidone, magnesium stearate EXC-A5 Amfexa / Dexamfetamine Sulfate Medice 10 mg Isomalt, magnesium stearate, yellow iron oxide EXC-A10 Amfexa / Dexamfetamine Sulfate Medice 20 mg Isomalt, magnesium stearate, red iron oxide EXC-A20 Brown & Burk dexamfetamine sulfate 5 mg Microcrystalline cellulose, calcium hydrogen phosphate dihydrate, povidone, maize starch, magnesium stearate EXC-BB Clinical guidance These documents list different excipients in tablets containing dexamfetamine sulfate. They do not establish that a particular excipient causes reduced benefit or that one tablet is more effective. EXC-A5 EXC-A10 EXC-A20 EXC-BB Povidone and crospovidone are related but distinct ingredients. Do not use their names interchangeably. The manufacturer of the earlier generic product in my personal account has not been established here; the Brown & Burk entry is a verified example, not an identification of what I was dispensed. Some local NHS agreements advise prescribing dexamfetamine by brand. That is a local prescribing instruction, not proof of a universal clinical difference. P1 Elvanse has a different delivery route Lisdexamfetamine is a prodrug: the body converts it into active dexamfetamine. The product information identifies blood, primarily red blood cells, as the main conversion setting. It also describes substantial conversion capacity in laboratory measurements. EXC-LDX Clinical guidance Poor real-world benefit does not by itself demonstrate failed lisdexamfetamine activation. A subjective effect, a measured blood concentration and everyday functional capacity answer different questions. EXC-LDX The established conversion route does not support an assertion that an energetically inefficient nervous system necessarily makes Elvanse break down unpredictably. A person can still experience incomplete or inconsistent benefit that deserves clinical review. The uncertainty belongs in the explanation, not in whether the experience is worth listening to. A record you can bring to a review Keep this small enough to use: product and strength; what changed; time taken; function improved or not improved; unwanted effects; what else was different. Dates and a photograph of the pack can be more useful than a long account reconstructed later. If useful, add the PL number, time of first noticeable benefit, duration, sleep and meals. Record contradictory days as well as days that fit an explanation. For suspected adverse reactions, the MHRA Yellow Card scheme accepts reports. If there is facial or throat swelling, difficulty breathing or collapse, seek emergency help rather than trying the product again yourself. Uncertainty An ingredient-list comparison identifies formulation differences. It does not diagnose hypersensitivity, establish altered absorption or prove why a medicine helped one person less. A poor response should be evaluated without treating every proposed mechanism as established. Unresolved sources The manufacturer and exact formulation of my earlier generic tablets remain to be checked against dispensing records. European regulatory information recognises that some excipients can have effects in particular circumstances and requires corresponding ingredient and safety information. This supports checking the actual formulation; it does not demonstrate the cause of one person's poor response.
The following comparison uses the named UK manufacturer documents checked on 14 October 2026. It concerns ingredient lists, not comparative efficacy.
Isomalt, magnesium stearate, yellow iron oxide
Isomalt, magnesium stearate, red iron oxide
Microcrystalline cellulose, calcium hydrogen phosphate dihydrate, povidone, maize starch, magnesium stearate
These documents list different excipients in tablets containing dexamfetamine sulfate. They do not establish that a particular excipient causes reduced benefit or that one tablet is more effective.

Povidone and crospovidone are related but distinct ingredients. Do not use their names interchangeably. The manufacturer of the earlier generic product in my personal account has not been established here; the Brown & Burk entry is a verified example, not an identification of what I was dispensed.
Some local NHS agreements advise prescribing dexamfetamine by brand. That is a local prescribing instruction, not proof of a universal clinical difference.
Elvanse has a different delivery route

Lisdexamfetamine is a prodrug: the body converts it into active dexamfetamine. The product information identifies blood, primarily red blood cells, as the main conversion setting. It also describes substantial conversion capacity in laboratory measurements.

Poor real-world benefit does not by itself demonstrate failed lisdexamfetamine activation. A subjective effect, a measured blood concentration and everyday functional capacity answer different questions.

The established conversion route does not support an assertion that an energetically inefficient nervous system necessarily makes Elvanse break down unpredictably. A person can still experience incomplete or inconsistent benefit that deserves clinical review. The uncertainty belongs in the explanation, not in whether the experience is worth listening to.
A record you can bring to a review
Keep this small enough to use:
product and strength; what changed; time taken; function improved or not improved; unwanted effects; what else was different.
Dates and a photograph of the pack can be more useful than a long account reconstructed later.
If useful, add the PL number, time of first noticeable benefit, duration, sleep and meals. Record contradictory days as well as days that fit an explanation.
accepts reports. If there is facial or throat swelling, difficulty breathing or collapse, seek emergency help rather than trying the product again yourself.

An ingredient-list comparison identifies formulation differences. It does not diagnose hypersensitivity, establish altered absorption or prove why a medicine helped one person less. A poor response should be evaluated without treating every proposed mechanism as established.
The manufacturer and exact formulation of my earlier generic tablets remain to be checked against dispensing records.
