articles.text: Science / Practical · GEN-09 Family history and inheritance patterns Last updated 30 September 2026 GEN-09 On this page What mitochondrial biology can explain What needs distinguishing Inheritance patterns in plain English How to collect a useful family history What a negative family history does and does not mean What this evidence can tell us Sources What mitochondrial biology can explain A good family history is one of the cheapest, most useful things you can give a clinician. It tells them which inheritance pattern to look for and which tests are worth requesting. ADHD clusters in families but does not follow a simple single-gene pattern. Some rare movement conditions do. What needs distinguishing "Nobody else in my family has it, so it cannot be genetic." Not so. A variant can arise for the first time in you ( de novo ), sit silently in both parents (recessive), or show up weakly or not at all in relatives (reduced penetrance ). Relatives may also be undiagnosed, especially in older generations. Inheritance patterns in plain English Pattern What it looks like in a family Example in this series Autosomal dominant One changed copy is enough. Can appear in every generation Dominant GCH1 deficiency, the commonest dopa-responsive dystonia form [ 1 ] Autosomal recessive Two changed copies needed. Parents usually unaffected carriers. Often skips generations Recessive GCH1 deficiency [ 2 ] ; most reported SPG7-related disease ( not yet verified ) X-linked Passed on the X chromosome. Affects males more obviously Not a main pattern in this series De novo New in the affected person, absent in both parents Rare damaging variants in ADHD [ 3 ] Polygenic (many small effects) Clusters in families with no clean pattern Typical ADHD [ 4 ] Two ideas that explain "missing" family history Reduced penetrance. Some carriers never develop symptoms. In the dominant GCH1 form, symptoms are more common in females, and most asymptomatic adult carriers were male [ 1 ] . A parent can carry the variant while seeming unaffected. Variable expressivity. Carriers of the same variant can be mildly or severely affected, or affected in different ways. How to collect a useful family history Aim for three generations: you, parents, siblings, grandparents, aunts, uncles, cousins and children. For each person, note the following. Question Why it helps Relationship and age, or age at death Places them on the tree Any diagnosed condition, and at what age it started Age of onset separates inheritance patterns Walking, stiffness, tremor, falls, "clumsy" or "tight" legs; symptoms that vary through the day Flags movement disorders, including dopa-responsive types ADHD, autism, dyslexia, learning difficulties, or "never diagnosed but obviously" Shows neurodevelopmental clustering Any genetic tests and their results Avoids repeating work Parents who are blood relatives, or shared ancestry or region Raises the chance of recessive conditions Response to medicines (what helped, what made things worse) Can echo across relatives Early deaths, and causes May reveal undiagnosed conditions Keep it factual. Record what is known and mark guesses as guesses. A clinician can work with "uncle, walked stiffly from his thirties, never diagnosed". What a negative family history does and does not mean It lowers the odds of some dominant conditions but does not exclude recessive, de novo or reduced-penetrance conditions, nor relatives' undiagnosed disease. Clinicians weigh it alongside examination and tests. What this evidence can tell us This page explains patterns; it does not say what pattern any family has. The reduced-penetrance statement applies to dominant GCH1 deficiency as reported in the MDSGene review [ 1 ] . Other conditions differ. ADHD is not inherited like a single-gene condition [ 4 ] . c: How to collect a useful family history
What a negative family history does and does not mean
What this evidence can tell us

A good family history is one of the cheapest, most useful things you can give a clinician. It tells them which inheritance pattern to look for and which tests are worth requesting. ADHD clusters in families but does not follow a simple single-gene pattern. Some rare movement conditions do.
"Nobody else in my family has it, so it cannot be genetic." Not so. A variant can arise for the first time in you (

a.title: New in a person, not inherited from either parent

c: ), sit silently in both parents (recessive), or show up weakly or not at all in relatives (reduced

a.title: The share of carriers who develop the condition. "Reduced penetrance" means some carriers never do

c: ). Relatives may also be undiagnosed, especially in older generations.
What it looks like in a family
One changed copy is enough. Can appear in every generation

a.title: A group of conditions, often involving the GCH1 or TH genes, in which symptoms improve markedly with low-dose levodopa

c: Two changed copies needed. Parents usually unaffected carriers. Often skips generations
Passed on the X chromosome. Affects males more obviously
Not a main pattern in this series
New in the affected person, absent in both parents
Clusters in families with no clean pattern
Two ideas that explain "missing" family history
Some carriers never develop symptoms. In the dominant GCH1 form, symptoms are more common in females, and most asymptomatic adult carriers were male
. A parent can carry the variant while seeming unaffected.
Carriers of the same variant can be mildly or severely affected, or affected in different ways.
How to collect a useful family history
Aim for three generations: you, parents, siblings, grandparents, aunts, uncles, cousins and children. For each person, note the following.
Relationship and age, or age at death
Any diagnosed condition, and at what age it started
Age of onset separates inheritance patterns
Walking, stiffness, tremor, falls, "clumsy" or "tight" legs; symptoms that vary through the day
Flags movement disorders, including dopa-responsive types
ADHD, autism, dyslexia, learning difficulties, or "never diagnosed but obviously"
Any genetic tests and their results
Parents who are blood relatives, or shared ancestry or region
Raises the chance of recessive conditions
Response to medicines (what helped, what made things worse)
Record what is known and mark guesses as guesses. A clinician can work with "uncle, walked stiffly from his thirties, never diagnosed".
What a negative family history does and does not mean

It lowers the odds of some dominant conditions but does not exclude recessive, de novo or reduced-penetrance conditions, nor relatives' undiagnosed disease. Clinicians weigh it alongside examination and tests.
What this evidence can tell us
This page explains patterns; it does not say what pattern any family has.

articles.text: Confirmed science / Genetics · GEN-10 Autism genetics in brief Last updated 30 September 2026 GEN-10 On this page What functional evidence adds What needs distinguishing The plain-English layer The medical-care evidence What this evidence can tell us Sources What functional evidence adds Autism is strongly heritable. A large five-country register study estimated a median heritability of about 81% (range 73-86%) [ 1 ] . ADHD and autism often occur together and share some genetic liability ( Tier B ; exact overlap figures not yet verified ). In a Swedish register study, autistic people died at higher rates than matched controls across almost every diagnostic category, from a wide range of medical causes [ 2 ] . Both facts point the same way for care: these are lifelong neurodevelopmental conditions with medical consequences. They are not conditions that belong only under mental health services. What needs distinguishing "Autism and ADHD are separate, so their genetics are separate." They are separate diagnoses with overlapping biology. A person can have both, and current diagnostic manuals allow both to be recorded together ( not yet verified ). The plain-English layer Heritability The Bai et al. study pooled data on 2,001,631 individuals, including 22,156 with autism, across five countries. The median heritability was 80.8% (range 73.2-85.5%), and the maternal effect was small (0.4-1.6%) [ 1 ] . As with ADHD ( GEN-01 ), heritability describes why people differ in a population. It does not describe a share of any one person's autism. Genetic architecture As with ADHD, autism involves many common variants of small effect and rarer variants of larger effect, including new ( de novo ) variants ( Tier B , general; not yet verified for gene counts). GEN-04 explains the difference. What genes say about needs Genes do not tell you a person's support needs. Autistic people vary enormously in communication, independence and health needs, and no gene result predicts those for an individual. The medical-care evidence The Swedish study followed 27,122 people diagnosed with autism between 1987 and 2009 against 2,672,185 matched controls. During follow-up, 706 autistic people (2.60%) had died compared with 0.91% of the general population (odds ratio 2.56; 95% CI 2.38-2.76). Mortality was raised for almost all diagnostic categories, with sex and general intellectual ability moderating the pattern [ 2 ] . The authors concluded that premature mortality was markedly increased owing to a multitude of medical conditions. Why this belongs in a genetics series. If a neurodevelopmental condition is associated with raised risk across many medical causes, then care cannot be organised as if the condition were only a mental-health matter. Whole-person medical care, with clear ownership, is the evidence-consistent model. The policy argument is developed in the policy section of this site. What this evidence can tell us Register studies show association, not cause. The mortality study is Swedish and covers diagnoses made between 1987 and 2009; care systems and diagnostic practice have changed since. The 81% figure is a pooled estimate across countries and designs; individual studies differ. The overlap between ADHD and autism genetics is stated here only in general terms until the source figures are verified. Nothing here is advice about any individual's diagnosis or needs. Sources Bibliographic details checked against PubMed. Bai D et al. Association of genetic and environmental factors with autism in a 5-country cohort. JAMA Psychiatry 2019;76(10):1035-1043. articles.text: Confirmed science / Reference · GEN-11 Genetics glossary Last updated 30 September 2026 GEN-11 On this page Terms you will meet Terms What this evidence can tell us Sources Terms you will meet Short, plain definitions for the terms used in the GEN series. If a term is missing, it should be added here with a one-line definition and linked from the article that uses it. Terms Term Plain-English meaning AADC (aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase; gene DDC) The enzyme that turns L-DOPA into dopamine Allele One version of a gene or DNA variant. You have two copies of most genes, one from each parent Autosomal dominant One changed copy is enough to cause the condition Autosomal recessive Two changed copies are needed; parents are usually unaffected carriers Basal ganglia Deep brain structures involved in movement and habit, and heavily dependent on dopamine BH4 (tetrahydrobiopterin) A helper molecule that tyrosine hydroxylase needs to make L-DOPA. The enzyme GCH1 controls the rate-limiting step of making it Candidate gene A gene chosen in advance because it seemed plausible. Studies of candidate genes are older and less reliable than genome-wide ones Carrier Someone who has a changed copy of a gene CNV (copy-number variant) A stretch of DNA that is missing or repeated De novo New in a person, not inherited from either parent DAT (dopamine transporter; gene SLC6A3, old name DAT1) The protein that pulls dopamine back into the cell after release Differential diagnosis The list of conditions a clinician is weighing and needs to rule in or out Dystonia Sustained or repeated muscle contractions that cause twisting movements or abnormal postures Dopa-responsive dystonia (DRD) A group of conditions, often involving the GCH1 or TH genes, in which symptoms improve markedly with low-dose levodopa Effector gene The gene in a risk region that is thought to actually drive the effect. Proposed by computer methods and needs confirmation Exome The protein-coding parts of the genome Expressivity How strongly or in what way a variant shows up in a person GWAS (genome-wide association study) A study that scans the whole genome in many people to find common DNA differences linked to a trait Heritability The proportion of differences in a trait across a population that is explained by genetic differences. It is not the proportion of any one person's condition Heterozygous Having one changed copy and one typical copy of a gene Homozygous Having two identical copies of a variant HSP (hereditary spastic paraplegia) A group of inherited conditions causing progressive stiffness and weakness in the legs Liability An underlying tendency toward a condition, spread across a population. Diagnosis is thought of as the point where liability passes a threshold Levodopa (L-DOPA) The precursor that the body converts to dopamine. Used as a medicine and as a diagnostic clue Locus (plural loci) A region of DNA MAO / COMT Enzymes that break down dopamine and related chemicals Penetrance The share of carriers who develop the condition. "Reduced penetrance" means some carriers never do Pharmacogenomics The study of how genes change the way the body handles a drug Polygenic Influenced by many genes, each with a small effect Polygenic score (PGS) A number that adds up many small DNA effects into one risk estimate for a person Proband The first person in a family to be identified with a condition Rate-limiting step The slowest step in a chain, which sets the pace of the whole pathway SNP (single-nucleotide polymorphism) A change in a single DNA letter that is common in the population SNP heritability The share of heritability explained by common variants Spasticity Muscle stiffness caused by a fault in the nervous-system control of muscle tone, often with exaggerated reflexes TH (tyrosine hydroxylase) The rate-limiting enzyme in dopamine production Trio A child and both parents sequenced together, to find new ( de novo ) variants Twin study Comparing identical with non-identical twins to estimate how much of a trait is genetic V-ATPase A pump that uses ATP to build a proton gradient across a vesicle's membrane. VMAT2 uses that gradient to pack dopamine into the vesicle Variant A difference in DNA from the typical sequence VMAT2 (vesicular monoamine transporter 2; gene SLC18A2) The protein that loads dopamine, serotonin and noradrenaline into storage vesicles VNTR A stretch of DNA made of a repeating unit. The number of repeats varies between people. DAT1 and DRD4 have well-known ones VUS (variant of uncertain significance) A DNA change where there is not enough evidence to call it harmful or harmless. Not a diagnosis Vesicle A tiny bubble inside a nerve cell that stores chemical messengers ready for release What this evidence can tell us Definitions are simplified for readability. articles.text: Confirmed science / Genetics · GEN-12 The 27 ADHD risk loci: a closer look Last updated 5 October 2026 GEN-12 On this page What the 27 loci represent How to use the locus links Locus index The 27 regions in detail What needs distinguishing The deeper layer (optional to read) What this evidence can tell us Sources What the 27 loci represent Demontis and colleagues reported 27 genome-wide significant ADHD risk regions in a 2023 analysis of 38,691 cases and 186,843 controls. Each row below is a region anchored by an index variant, not a confirmed causal gene or a diagnostic result. The paper reports 32 independent lead variants across these 27 regions; this guide follows its Table 1, one entry per region [ 1 ] . A different 2025 analysis incorporating childhood symptom scores reported 39 loci under its own study design. The counts should not be added together or read as a simple time series. See GEN-01 for the broader context [ 2 ] . How to use the locus links Select a locus in the index to jump to its entry. Chromosome positions use the paper’s hg19 reference assembly. The listed genes are within 50 kb of the index variant in Table 1; an empty cell means that table listed none in that window. The odds ratio is for effect allele A1, comparing alleles in this study, and is not an individual prediction. P values describe association evidence, not the size or clinical meaning of an effect [ 1 ] . articles.text: Confirmed science / Genetics Genetics and ADHD: start here Last updated 30 September 2026 GEN-00 On this page Choose a genetics topic What needs distinguishing Reading order How every article in the series is built Evidence tiers used in this series What this evidence can tell us Sources Choose a genetics topic ADHD runs in families. Twin studies put heritability at about 74% ( Tier B ). There is no single "ADHD gene". The picture is thousands of common variants that each nudge risk a tiny amount, plus rarer variants with bigger effects, plus chance and environment ( Tier B ). Genes describe risk . They are not a diagnostic test and they do not tell a clinician which medication to use ( Tier B ). Some rare single-gene conditions affect the same dopamine pathways and can produce movement symptoms. That is a differential diagnosis question for specialists, not proof that ADHD is caused by those genes ( Tier A for the conditions, Tier D for any link to ADHD). Schematic, not a data chart Two studies, two counts. Demontis and colleagues (2023) reported 27 genome-wide significant regions from ADHD diagnosis data ( DOI ). van der Laan and colleagues (2025) combined childhood symptom scores with diagnosis data and reported 39, of which 17 were new ( DOI ). The designs differ, so the counts are not a running total, and neither is a personal score. Details in GEN-01 and GEN-12 . What needs distinguishing "It's genetic" gets heard as "one faulty gene". The real finding is closer to "many small dials and a few large switches". Keeping those two pictures apart is the whole point of this series. articles.title: The dopamine pathway, step by step
articles.description: An explorable map of how a brain dopamine cell makes, stores, releases and clears dopamine, with sources and limits for every step.
articles.statusNote: Body, figures and links extracted from the pinned file. Wording was not rewritten.
articles.text: Confirmed science / Mechanism The dopamine pathway, step by step Last updated 5 October 2026 Model 1.0.0 The short version This is a map of how one dopamine-releasing nerve cell in the brain makes, stores and releases dopamine, and of what then happens to the dopamine. Each box is a step, a supporting ingredient, a feedback brake or a related pathway. The biology of each step is well established ( Tier A ). Whether a weak step explains ADHD in any particular person is an open question ( Tier D ), and the map does not answer it. How to use it. Select any box to read about it in the panel below the map. Selecting a box only changes what you are reading. It does not measure, test or change anything, and it cannot tell you whether you have ADHD or which medicine might suit you. The map Solid arrow: next step in the sequence Dotted: cofactor or energy support Dashed: feedback (a brake) Thin: related pathway, for context Every step as text Main line: inside a brain dopamine cell Tyrosine supply Step · The starting material, from the blood. What happens Tyrosine, an amino acid, is the starting material for dopamine. It comes from protein in food, and the body can also make it from another amino acid, phenylalanine, using the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH). Tier A Connections → Entry into the brain : Tyrosine in the blood is carried into the brain by LAT1. (solid arrow) → Outside the brain : The same starting material and enzymes are also used outside the brain. (thin line) ADHD research No established link (GEN-03). Phenylketonuria (PKU), where PAH does not work, is a separate condition. Limits This map is not diet advice. It does not show that eating more protein or taking tyrosine changes ADHD symptoms. Sources [1] Abstract Read more Related article Entry into the brain Step · Crossing the blood–brain barrier. What happens To reach brain nerve cells, tyrosine has to cross the blood–brain barrier. It uses LAT1 (gene SLC7A5), a carrier for large neutral amino acids, and competes for it with other amino acids of that type, such as phenylalanine. Tier A Connections → Tyrosine to L-DOPA : Tyrosine inside the brain is the starting material for tyrosine hydroxylase. (solid arrow) ← Tyrosine supply : Tyrosine in the blood is carried into the brain by LAT1. (solid arrow) ADHD research Open research question, not established (GEN-03). Tier D Limits The LAT1 statement comes from the discussion section of a rat and mouse study and describes the transporter's general role. Sources [2] Discussion; [1] Biochemical markers for assessment of metabolic control; Functional effect of Phe-free L-amino acid supplements Read more Related article Tyrosine to L-DOPA Step · Rate-limiting step, by tyrosine hydroxylase. What happens The enzyme tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) converts tyrosine to L-DOPA. It is the rate-limiting step: the slowest, most tightly controlled step in making dopamine and the other catecholamines. Tier A Needs BH4 (tetrahydrobiopterin), oxygen, and iron held in the enzyme. Connections → L-DOPA to dopamine : Tyrosine hydroxylase's product, L-DOPA, is converted to dopamine by AADC. (solid arrow) ← Entry into the brain : Tyrosine inside the brain is the starting material for tyrosine hydroxylase. (solid arrow) ← BH4 helper molecule : Tyrosine hydroxylase needs BH4 to work. (dotted line) ← Autoreceptor feedback : Autoreceptor activity reduces dopamine synthesis. (dashed line) ← L-DOPA to dopamine : Dopamine and other catecholamines inhibit tyrosine hydroxylase (end-product feedback). (dashed line) ADHD research None established (GEN-03). None of the 27 regions in the 2023 genome-wide study lists TH within 50 kb (GEN-12). Medicines that act here Levodopa, used mainly for Parkinson's disease, supplies L-DOPA directly and so does not depend on this step (GEN-03). For understanding only; not a treatment guide. Limits “Rate-limiting” describes how much dopamine is made. How strongly dopamine signals also depends on packaging, release, receptors and clearance. Sources [3] Abstract Read more Related article L-DOPA to dopamine Step · Conversion by AADC. What happens The enzyme aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (AADC, gene DDC) converts L-DOPA to dopamine. Tier A Needs PLP (pyridoxal phosphate), the active form of vitamin B6. Connections → Packaging into vesicles : Newly made dopamine is loaded into vesicles by VMAT2. (solid arrow) → Tyrosine to L-DOPA : Dopamine and other catecholamines inhibit tyrosine hydroxylase (end-product feedback). (dashed line) ← Tyrosine to L-DOPA : Tyrosine hydroxylase's product, L-DOPA, is converted to dopamine by AADC. (solid arrow) ← Vitamin B6 (PLP) : AADC needs PLP to work. (dotted line) ADHD research None established (GEN-03). None of the 27 regions in the 2023 genome-wide study lists DDC within 50 kb (GEN-12). Limits AADC deficiency is a rare inherited condition. It is mentioned to show that this step matters, not as an explanation of ADHD. Sources [3] Introduction; [4] Abstract; Lumbar puncture Read more Related article Packaging into vesicles Step · Loaded into storage sacs by VMAT2. What happens VMAT2 (gene SLC18A2) loads dopamine from inside the cell into vesicles, the small sacs that store it ready for release. Tier A Needs A proton gradient across the vesicle wall, built by the vesicle's proton pump. Connections → Release : Filled vesicles release dopamine when calcium enters the nerve ending. (solid arrow) → Noradrenaline branch : In noradrenaline cells, dopamine inside vesicles is converted to noradrenaline by DBH. (thin line) ← L-DOPA to dopamine : Newly made dopamine is loaded into vesicles by VMAT2. (solid arrow) ← Vesicle proton pump : VMAT2 uses the proton gradient built by the vesicle's proton pump. (dotted line) ADHD research One small platelet study (GEN-03 rates this Tier C). None of the 27 regions in the 2023 genome-wide study lists SLC18A2 within 50 kb (GEN-12). Tier C Medicines that act here Amphetamine inhibits VMAT2, which releases dopamine from vesicle storage. Methylphenidate is reported to redistribute VMAT2. For understanding only; not a treatment guide. Limits After release, vesicles are recycled and refilled; that cycle is not drawn as a separate step. Sources [5] Abstract; [6] Amphetamine; Methylphenidate; [7] Figure 2 legend Read more Related article Release Step · Calcium triggers vesicles to release dopamine. What happens When an electrical signal reaches the nerve ending, calcium flows in and triggers vesicles to fuse with the cell membrane, releasing dopamine into the gap between cells. Tier A Connections → Receptors : Released dopamine binds receptors on nearby cells. (solid arrow) → Reuptake : Released dopamine is carried back into the releasing cell, mainly by DAT in the striatum. (solid arrow) → Breakdown : Released dopamine is broken down by MAO and COMT. (solid arrow) → Autoreceptor feedback : Released dopamine also binds D2 autoreceptors on the releasing cell. (solid arrow) ← Packaging into vesicles : Filled vesicles release dopamine when calcium enters the nerve ending. (solid arrow) ← Autoreceptor feedback : Autoreceptor activity reduces dopamine release. (dashed line) ADHD research No specific link stated on this site. Medicines that act here Amphetamine can also move dopamine out of the cell by making the transporter DAT run in reverse (see Reuptake). For understanding only; not a treatment guide. Limits Release is adjusted moment to moment by the cell's activity and by autoreceptor feedback. Sources [7] Abstract Read more Related article Supports: cofactors and energy BH4 helper molecule Support (cofactor or energy) · Cofactor for tyrosine hydroxylase. What happens Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) is a helper molecule (cofactor) that tyrosine hydroxylase needs. BH4 has its own rate-limiting step, made by the enzyme GTP cyclohydrolase I (GCH1). Tier A Connections → Tyrosine to L-DOPA : Tyrosine hydroxylase needs BH4 to work. (dotted line) ADHD research None established. GCH1 conditions are movement disorders (see GEN-06). Limits A support link, not a step in the sequence. Sources [3] Abstract Read more Related article Vitamin B6 (PLP) Support (cofactor or energy) · Cofactor for AADC. What happens Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), the active form of vitamin B6, is the cofactor AADC needs to convert L-DOPA to dopamine. Tier A Connections → L-DOPA to dopamine : AADC needs PLP to work. (dotted line) ADHD research None established. Limits A support link, not a step. This map does not give supplement advice. Sources [4] Lumbar puncture Read more Related article Vesicle proton pump Support (cofactor or energy) · Builds the gradient VMAT2 uses. What happens A pump in the vesicle wall, the vesicular proton ATPase (V-ATPase), uses ATP to push protons into the vesicle, making it acidic and charged inside. Vesicle transporters, including VMAT2, use this gradient to load their transmitter. Tier A Needs ATP. Connections → Packaging into vesicles : VMAT2 uses the proton gradient built by the vesicle's proton pump. (dotted line) ← Energy (ATP) : The proton pump uses ATP. (dotted line) ADHD research None established. Limits The pump is not driven directly by the mitochondria's own proton gradient; energy supply matters through ATP (GEN-03). Sources [8] Abstract; Vesicular Synergy of VNTs Read more Related article Energy (ATP) Support (cofactor or energy) · Powers the proton pump. What happens ATP is the cell's energy currency. The vesicle's proton pump is an ATPase: it uses ATP to do its work. Tier A Connections → Vesicle proton pump : The proton pump uses ATP. (dotted line) ADHD research None established. Limits This is not a measure of anyone's energy, tiredness or “battery level”. Sources [8] Abstract Read more Related article After release Receptors Step · Dopamine binds receptors on nearby cells. What happens Released dopamine binds dopamine receptors on nearby cells. There are five types, D1 to D5, grouped as D1-like (D1 and D5) and D2-like (D2, D3 and D4). Tier A Connections ← Release : Released dopamine binds receptors on nearby cells. (solid arrow) ADHD research Older candidate-gene studies reported signals for DRD4 and DRD5, with heterogeneity, before genome-wide studies (GEN-03). None of the 27 regions in the 2023 genome-wide study lists DRD4 or DRD5 within 50 kb. c: The dopamine pathway, step by step

This is a map of how one dopamine-releasing nerve cell in the brain makes, stores and releases dopamine, and of what then happens to the dopamine. Each box is a step, a supporting ingredient, a feedback brake or a related pathway. The biology of each step is well established (
). Whether a weak step explains ADHD in any particular person is an open question (
), and the map does not answer it.

Select any box to read about it in the panel below the map. Selecting a box only changes what you are reading. It does not measure, test or change anything, and it cannot tell you whether you have ADHD or which medicine might suit you.
Solid arrow: next step in the sequence
Main line: inside a brain dopamine cell
Step · The starting material, from the blood.

Tyrosine, an amino acid, is the starting material for dopamine. It comes from protein in food, and the body can also make it from another amino acid, phenylalanine, using the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH).
: Tyrosine in the blood is carried into the brain by LAT1.
: The same starting material and enzymes are also used outside the brain.
No established link (GEN-03). Phenylketonuria (PKU), where PAH does not work, is a separate condition.
This map is not diet advice. It does not show that eating more protein or taking tyrosine changes ADHD symptoms.

To reach brain nerve cells, tyrosine has to cross the blood–brain barrier. It uses LAT1 (gene SLC7A5), a carrier for large neutral amino acids, and competes for it with other amino acids of that type, such as phenylalanine.
: Tyrosine inside the brain is the starting material for tyrosine hydroxylase.
: Tyrosine in the blood is carried into the brain by LAT1.
The LAT1 statement comes from the discussion section of a rat and mouse study and describes the transporter's general role.
Biochemical markers for assessment of metabolic control; Functional effect of Phe-free L-amino acid supplements
Step · Rate-limiting step, by tyrosine hydroxylase.
The enzyme tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) converts tyrosine to L-DOPA. It is the rate-limiting step: the slowest, most tightly controlled step in making dopamine and the other catecholamines.
BH4 (tetrahydrobiopterin), oxygen, and iron held in the enzyme.
: Tyrosine hydroxylase's product, L-DOPA, is converted to dopamine by AADC.
: Tyrosine inside the brain is the starting material for tyrosine hydroxylase.
: Tyrosine hydroxylase needs BH4 to work.
: Dopamine and other catecholamines inhibit tyrosine hydroxylase (end-product feedback).
None established (GEN-03). None of the 27 regions in the 2023 genome-wide study lists TH within 50 kb (GEN-12).
Levodopa, used mainly for Parkinson's disease, supplies L-DOPA directly and so does not depend on this step (GEN-03).
For understanding only; not a treatment guide.
“Rate-limiting” describes how much dopamine is made. How strongly dopamine signals also depends on packaging, release, receptors and clearance.
The enzyme aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (AADC, gene DDC) converts L-DOPA to dopamine.
PLP (pyridoxal phosphate), the active form of vitamin B6.
: Newly made dopamine is loaded into vesicles by VMAT2.
: Dopamine and other catecholamines inhibit tyrosine hydroxylase (end-product feedback).
: Tyrosine hydroxylase's product, L-DOPA, is converted to dopamine by AADC.
None established (GEN-03). None of the 27 regions in the 2023 genome-wide study lists DDC within 50 kb (GEN-12).
AADC deficiency is a rare inherited condition. It is mentioned to show that this step matters, not as an explanation of ADHD.
Step · Loaded into storage sacs by VMAT2.
VMAT2 (gene SLC18A2) loads dopamine from inside the cell into vesicles, the small sacs that store it ready for release.
A proton gradient across the vesicle wall, built by the vesicle's proton pump.
: Filled vesicles release dopamine when calcium enters the nerve ending.
: In noradrenaline cells, dopamine inside vesicles is converted to noradrenaline by DBH.
: Newly made dopamine is loaded into vesicles by VMAT2.
: VMAT2 uses the proton gradient built by the vesicle's proton pump.
One small platelet study (GEN-03 rates this Tier C). None of the 27 regions in the 2023 genome-wide study lists SLC18A2 within 50 kb (GEN-12).
Amphetamine inhibits VMAT2, which releases dopamine from vesicle storage. Methylphenidate is reported to redistribute VMAT2.
For understanding only; not a treatment guide.
After release, vesicles are recycled and refilled; that cycle is not drawn as a separate step.
Step · Calcium triggers vesicles to release dopamine.
When an electrical signal reaches the nerve ending, calcium flows in and triggers vesicles to fuse with the cell membrane, releasing dopamine into the gap between cells.
: Released dopamine binds receptors on nearby cells.
: Released dopamine is carried back into the releasing cell, mainly by DAT in the striatum.
: Released dopamine is broken down by MAO and COMT.
: Released dopamine also binds D2 autoreceptors on the releasing cell.
: Filled vesicles release dopamine when calcium enters the nerve ending.
No specific link stated on this site.
Amphetamine can also move dopamine out of the cell by making the transporter DAT run in reverse (see Reuptake).
For understanding only; not a treatment guide.
Release is adjusted moment to moment by the cell's activity and by autoreceptor feedback.
Support (cofactor or energy) · Cofactor for tyrosine hydroxylase.
Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) is a helper molecule (cofactor) that tyrosine hydroxylase needs. BH4 has its own rate-limiting step, made by the enzyme GTP cyclohydrolase I (GCH1).
: Tyrosine hydroxylase needs BH4 to work.
None established. GCH1 conditions are movement disorders (see GEN-06).
A support link, not a step in the sequence.
Support (cofactor or energy) · Cofactor for AADC.
Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), the active form of vitamin B6, is the cofactor AADC needs to convert L-DOPA to dopamine.
A support link, not a step. This map does not give supplement advice.
Support (cofactor or energy) · Builds the gradient VMAT2 uses.

A pump in the vesicle wall, the vesicular proton ATPase (V-ATPase), uses ATP to push protons into the vesicle, making it acidic and charged inside. Vesicle transporters, including VMAT2, use this gradient to load their transmitter.
: VMAT2 uses the proton gradient built by the vesicle's proton pump.
The pump is not driven directly by the mitochondria's own proton gradient; energy supply matters through ATP (GEN-03).
Support (cofactor or energy) · Powers the proton pump.
ATP is the cell's energy currency. The vesicle's proton pump is an ATPase: it uses ATP to do its work.
This is not a measure of anyone's energy, tiredness or “battery level”.
Step · Dopamine binds receptors on nearby cells.
Released dopamine binds dopamine receptors on nearby cells. There are five types, D1 to D5, grouped as D1-like (D1 and D5) and D2-like (D2, D3 and D4).
: Released dopamine binds receptors on nearby cells.

Older candidate-gene studies reported signals for DRD4 and DRD5, with heterogeneity, before genome-wide studies (GEN-03). None of the 27 regions in the 2023 genome-wide study lists DRD4 or DRD5 within 50 kb.
Some medicines act directly on dopamine receptors, such as drugs for Parkinson's disease and antipsychotics.
For understanding only; not a treatment guide.
Receptor signalling inside the receiving cell is not drawn.
Dopamine D2-autoreceptors – Location and Behavioral Function;
Step · DAT carries dopamine back into the cell.

After release, the dopamine transporter (DAT, gene SLC6A3) carries dopamine back into the releasing cell. In the striatum this is the main way released dopamine is cleared. In the frontal cortex DAT is sparse: mouse studies found that dopamine there is taken up mainly by the noradrenaline transporter (NET, gene SLC6A2).
: Released dopamine is carried back into the releasing cell, mainly by DAT in the striatum.
Candidate-gene signal for DAT1 (SLC6A3), with heterogeneity (GEN-03). None of the 27 regions in the 2023 genome-wide study lists SLC6A3 within 50 kb (GEN-12).
Methylphenidate inhibits DAT and NET. Amphetamine also inhibits these transporters and can make DAT run in reverse, moving dopamine out of the cell.
For understanding only; not a treatment guide.

The frontal-cortex finding comes from mouse studies; how closely it applies to people is less certain. How much dopamine taken back up is reused is not drawn, because it was not separately source-checked.
Step · MAO and COMT break dopamine down.
Dopamine is broken down by two enzyme families, monoamine oxidase (MAO) and catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT). In the mouse frontal cortex, COMT accounts for about half of dopamine clearance.
: Released dopamine is broken down by MAO and COMT.
No ADHD link is stated for MAO or COMT on GEN-03. None of the 27 regions in the 2023 genome-wide study lists COMT, MAOA or MAOB within 50 kb.
Amphetamine is reported to inhibit monoamine oxidase activity.
For understanding only; not a treatment guide.
The regional figure comes from a mouse study.
Feedback · A brake on the releasing cell.

Some released dopamine binds D2-type autoreceptors on the releasing cell itself. They act as a brake: feedback that controls the cell's firing and how much dopamine it makes, releases and takes back up.
: Released dopamine also binds D2 autoreceptors on the releasing cell.
No specific link stated on this site.
Feedback keeps the system within a working range. It is not a fixed personal set-point.
Related pathway (context) · One extra step in noradrenaline cells.

In noradrenaline-releasing nerve cells there is one extra step. Inside vesicles, the enzyme dopamine β-hydroxylase (DBH) converts dopamine to noradrenaline. This happens in the brain, in nerves elsewhere in the body, and in the adrenal gland.
: In noradrenaline cells, dopamine inside vesicles is converted to noradrenaline by DBH.
ADHD stimulant medicines act on the noradrenaline transporter (NET) as well as DAT.
Methylphenidate and amphetamine both inhibit NET.
For understanding only; not a treatment guide.
Shown for context. This page does not map the noradrenaline system in detail. DBH's own cofactors are not listed because they were not source-checked for this page.
Related pathway (context) · The same enzymes work elsewhere.

Tyrosine hydroxylase also works outside the brain, for example in the adrenal gland, which makes adrenaline. Levodopa taken as a medicine is mostly broken down in the body before it reaches the brain, mainly by AADC, so it is given with a peripheral AADC inhibitor such as carbidopa or benserazide.
: The same starting material and enzymes are also used outside the brain.
Not an ADHD finding; shown so that the brain line is not read as a universal rule.
Carbidopa and benserazide block AADC outside the brain so that more levodopa reaches it.
For understanding only; not a treatment guide.
“Entry into the brain, then conversion” is the order for brain dopamine cells only, not for the adrenal gland or other nerves.
What genetic studies do and do not show here
None of the genes on this map is listed within 50 kb of any of the 27 regions reported by the 2023 genome-wide study (
). Older candidate-gene studies reported signals for DAT1, DRD4 and DRD5, with heterogeneity between studies (
). An association with a region of DNA is not the same as a candidate gene, and neither is a proven causal mechanism (

Methylphenidate mainly inhibits the dopamine and noradrenaline transporters. Amphetamine also inhibits them, can make them run in reverse, and inhibits VMAT2. These notes explain why the medicines are discussed with this pathway. They are not a guide to choosing or changing treatment, which is a decision for a prescriber.
Limits and what is left out

MJB ADHD · original vector reconstruction · Reviewed 2026-10-13 Open larger diagram · Full-size PNG · Diagram page Read the diagram explanation and sources Two major organising processes are circadian timing and sleep homeostasis. Light helps synchronise circadian rhythms, while prior wakefulness contributes to sleep pressure. These interact with arousal systems and everyday context. Amphetamine acts as a substrate at monoamine transporters and can alter intracellular monoamine handling and support transporter-mediated efflux. Experimental work also identifies intracellular TAAR1 signalling and transporter trafficking. Vesicular stores affect availability, but knockout-culture evidence shows vesicular transport is not an absolute prerequisite for every experimental amphetamine action. Calcium-triggered exocytosis is therefore kept separate from efflux. Models, concentration and exposure conditions limit translation. The UK dexamfetamine SmPC does not claim a fully settled explanation of behavioural benefit in ADHD. No dose, efficacy, safety or individual mechanism is inferred.

articles.text: science What is ADHD? Last updated 30 September 2026 What ADHD means ADHD is a recognised neurodevelopmental condition described by persistent patterns of inattention and/or hyperactivity and impulsivity with functional impact. The outward pattern can differ across people, settings and life stages. A diagnosis requires a structured assessment; a single behaviour, questionnaire score or gene result does not establish it. Whole system overview An organising framework How do biology and context connect to cognitive function? This is an organising model, not one ADHD formula or a diagnostic graph. Sleep, stress and environment are additional inputs. The connecting arrows organise relationships for learning; they do not demonstrate one causal chain, one defect shared by everybody with ADHD or a diagnostic test. Demontis and colleagues 2023 ADHD GWAS Demontis and colleagues rare variants 2026 issue ADHD default mode mega analysis 2023 Rare genetic variants confer a high risk of ADHD and implicate neuronal biology (2025 online; 2026 issue) Attention is only part of it “A quiet or high-performing person cannot have ADHD.” A visible result cannot, on its own, explain the process behind it. Large scale brain networks Evidence interpretation Connectivity measures describe relationships in recorded brain activity. Dashed lines show statistical dependence, not axons or proven causal influence. MJB ADHD · original vector reconstruction · Reviewed 2026-10-13 Open larger diagram · Full-size PNG · Diagram page Read the diagram explanation and sources Functional connectivity quantifies statistical relationships between measured signals. It is distinct from an anatomical tract and from a demonstrated causal effect. ADHD studies examine group-level relationships among default-mode, attention, control and other networks; results vary with age, sample, task, motion and analysis. The network layout is conceptual, not a coordinate map or a faithful reproduction of a particular study result. Neither connectivity nor one network measure supplies a stand-alone diagnosis. Default-mode network → Control networks: statistical relation Default-mode network → Attention networks: statistical relation Control networks → Sensory and motor: statistical relation Attention networks → Sensory and motor: statistical relation ADHD default mode mega analysis 2023 ADHD multiscale functional connectivity 2025 Explore ADHD in more detail Look for the sustained cost of functioning across settings, including compensatory effort. What genes can and cannot tell you ADHD runs in families. Twin studies put heritability at about 74% ( Tier B ). That describes differences across a population, not a share of any one person's ADHD. There is no single “ADHD gene”. The picture is thousands of common variants that each nudge risk a tiny amount, plus rarer variants with bigger effects, plus chance and environment ( Tier B ). Genes describe risk . They are not a diagnostic test and they do not tell a clinician which medication to use ( Tier B ). Some rare single-gene conditions affect the same dopamine pathways and can produce movement symptoms. That is a differential diagnosis question for specialists, not proof that ADHD is caused by those genes ( Tier A for the conditions, Tier D for any link to ADHD). articles.text: Public source register · 30 September 2026 What supports which claim? The source, its date and its limit belong together. A national guideline states a general recommendation; a local policy records a procedure at a point in time; an individual account reports one experience. They answer different questions. Clinical and service context ADHD recognition and care: NICE NG87 recommendations , especially continuity of care. National guidance; it does not decide an individual prescription or determine fault in a case. System pathway concerns: NHS England, independent ADHD Taskforce report (2025; page updated 2026). A system review and recommendations, not evidence that a particular local action was implemented. Safe care framework: CQC guidance on Regulation 12 . A provider standard, not an individual regulatory finding. Disability threshold: Equality Act 2010, section 6 . The statutory definition depends on substantial, long-term effect; a diagnosis alone does not decide every adjustment. Historical local policy copies CWPT Complaints Policy v9.1 — supplied historical copy; check the trust's current route and deadlines. CWPT Safeguarding Adults Policy v5.0 — institutional policy, not a decision about any individual's threshold. CWPT Freedom to Speak Up Policy v6.5 — staff route, distinct from patient complaints. Coventry and Warwickshire ICB ADHD under-25 policy v3 — historical commissioning copy with an age scope; do not apply it to adult care or assume it remains current. First-person record and permitted commentary Journey and Accountability report a first-person chronology. Three original video files now accompany the accountability page. A clip records the speaker and date; it does not independently establish a clinical diagnosis, causation or the full institutional record. Professor Asherson, 24 August 2026 and 27 August extract and permission . His comments have the limits stated on the accountability page : he was not involved in care and did not have the full clinical details. Professor Shakespeare, 1 September 2026, extract and permission . A view on access and accommodation, not a judicial determination. Reading the pages Where an individual page reports a letter or meeting but the underlying personal record is not published, read it as the advocate's account. Private clinical letters and complaint submissions are not exposed here. How the source method works explains the distinction between source, claim, inference and proposed action. articles.title: How evidence is handled
articles.description: A plain-language method for sources, claims, uncertainty and corrections on MJB ADHD.
articles.statusNote: Body, figures and links extracted from the pinned file. Wording was not rewritten.
articles.text: Source control · work in progress How evidence is handled A document can show what was written. It cannot, by itself, show that a promised action happened. This site keeps those steps apart. Keep the source: record the issuer, title, version and date. Preserve an original when permission and privacy allow. State one claim at a time: attach the exact source and distinguish its words from a paraphrase. Mark the leap: separate documented fact, first-person account, inference, hypothesis and requested remedy. Keep the counterpoint: if a response disputes the claim, record it with its date and the specific issue it addresses. Check implementation: a response, review, assurance or promise is not a completed treatment, published pathway or closed action. articles.text: support When starting is the hard part Last updated 30 September 2026 Make the next step available A prompt, shared start time, visible next action or easier task environment can reduce friction. None is guaranteed, and effectiveness should be judged by whether the person’s function improves without an unsustainable effort cost. Understanding does not guarantee initiation “One failed tip means the person has not tried.” A visible result cannot, on its own, explain the process behind it. Illustration of lived experience, not a biological mechanism Many people describe a gap between deciding to do something and doing it. This drawing is a metaphor for that experience: the intention is there, but getting it through to action takes extra effort and arrives late. It is not a picture of brain activity, a transmitter level or a diagnosis, and it does not explain why the gap happens for any one person. For the biology that is actually established, see the dopamine pathway explorer . When understanding is not enough In this first-person account , I describe knowing what to do while losing the next action between pain, distraction and repeated attempts to begin. articles.title: When help doesn't come: get it in writing
articles.description: What to do when services do not act: text routes, keeping a written record, accessible ways to ask, and how to plan for the worst. Not medical or legal advice.
articles.statusNote: Body, figures and links extracted from the pinned file. Wording was not rewritten.
articles.text: support · safety When help doesn't come: get it in writing Last updated 5 October 2026 ⚠️ If you are in danger now Life at risk: call 999 or go to A&E. Urgent but not life-threatening: call NHS 111 and select the mental health option, or use 111 online . To talk: Samaritans, 116 123 , free, any time. To text: SHOUT to 85258 , free, confidential, 24/7. The short version Use text where you can, write everything down, and follow every call with a written note. If nothing happens, you still have a dated record showing who was told, when, and what they did or did not do. Never assume someone will do what they said they would do: check, and ask again in writing. 1. Use routes that leave a written record Text SHOUT to 85258. Free and confidential, 24/7, for anyone in the UK who is struggling to cope. Some NHS areas use their own keyword with the same number (for example CALMER in North East and North Cumbria); your local NHS trust or integrated care board website will say if yours does. Otherwise text SHOUT. Tell them plainly, in writing, what is happening and the effect your treatment, or the lack of it, is having on you. Can't use a voice call? articles.title: When understanding is not enough
articles.description: A first-person account of understanding a task while struggling to retain the next action, initiate it and manage pain and distraction.
articles.statusNote: Body, figures and links extracted from the pinned file. Wording was not rewritten.
articles.text: ADHD & daily life · Lived experience When understanding is not enough Matthew Bayliss · 14 October 2026 About this account: This describes my experience, not a definition of every person's ADHD or a clinical assessment. I can understand the whole task and still lose the next step “Executive dysfunction” sounds much tidier than it feels. I can understand a task, explain why it matters and work out how to do it. The difficulty comes when I have to keep the next action available long enough to start it, while pain, discomfort and distractions compete for the same limited attention. By the time I can initiate the action, I may have forgotten what it was. Then I have to reconstruct it. Find the instructions again. Work out where I stopped. Recover the intention. Try to begin. All of that is work, but from outside it can look as though nothing has happened. One active step is often all I can carry For me, a useful instruction looks like this: Open this named file. Wait for this specific screen. Press this labelled button. Each step needs to remain visible while I do it. I need to be able to return after an interruption and see exactly where I am. If I try to hold the whole plan in my head, I can lose both the plan and the action I was about to take. Sometimes two tightly connected actions fit together. More than that can mean standing there trying to remember everything and ending up with none of it available. Making instructions explicit saves me from repeatedly rebuilding the task. Something being obvious does not make it reliably accessible at the moment I need it. Pain makes the usable window smaller These difficulties happen even when I am lying down. Sitting at a computer adds discomfort and the effort of maintaining a position. My attention and endurance can become much worse. I described it as being useful for perhaps one minute out of every five. That is an estimate of how it feels, not a measured performance score. It captures the mismatch between the time I spend trying and the time in which I can actually move the task forward. A short setup can consume a long stretch of my day. The gaps between actions contain pain, distraction, lost intentions and repeated attempts to recover my place. Thinking and communicating have different costs My internal thinking can feel fast, connected and stimulating. Speaking requires me to turn that into a sequence someone else can follow, while listening, holding their contribution in mind and managing my body at the same time. Sometimes I have plenty I could say, but very little capacity left to say it. In conversations I cannot sustain, the words can become background noise while a tune or an internal thought stream takes over. Fighting to stay engaged can itself become exhausting. Being quiet, flat or apparently uninterested does not reliably tell someone how interested I am, how much I understand or how hard I am trying. I have been criticised for seeming miserable or uncommunicative while already struggling with pain and reduced access to things I found helpful. I experienced Amfexa as making it easier to participate and express myself, rather than spending so much effort manually getting through activity. That is my account of its benefit, not a recommendation about anyone else's medication or dose. Depth of understanding does not guarantee consistent output I can follow a complicated mechanism and make useful connections, yet struggle to retrieve a familiar word, organise an explanation or retain the next action. My writing may vary greatly in structure and clarity as my available capacity changes. The knowledge and the ability to present or act on it do not always arrive together. A fluent explanation on one occasion does not mean that capacity will be available on demand later. What makes a practical difference Show one active step, with the exact filename or button label. Keep my place visible and save progress automatically. Make it easy to stop and return without reconstructing the whole task. Let long processes continue without requiring my attention or an open conversation. Give me a clear result and one explicit next action. These changes reduce the amount I have to remember, recover and repeatedly initiate. They let more of my limited effort reach the task itself. Explore practical support.
